explanation.same-by-hand: Applicable. If two competent people always converge on the same answer from the same inputs, there's a rule being applied, not a judgment being made — that's the test to reach for on anything ambiguous.
explanation.one-page-rule: Applicable. If the whole mapping fits on one page, it's genuinely closed. A rule that would take a manual to state completely usually has exceptions folded into it that a one-page table can't capture.
explanation.high-volume: Not applicable as evidence the step is closed. Volume tells you a rules-engine replacement would be worth the effort — it's a reason to look, not evidence about what you'd find.
explanation.model-usually-right: Not applicable. A model can be highly accurate at a genuinely judgment-based task too — high accuracy tells you the model performs well, not that the underlying task was ever a closed mapping.
explanation.already-built: Not applicable, and worth naming directly: sunk cost isn't a signal about the task's nature. Whether the AI version already works and shipped has no bearing on whether the step was ever the kind of task a model was needed for.

contentSections.synthesis: The three signals that hold up are all about the mapping itself: is it fully specified, would two people agree, does it fit on one page. The three that don't are all about how the step performs or how much effort it would take to change — real considerations for a rollout plan, but not evidence about whether the step needed a model in the first place.

contentSections.body: Before asking whether a model is good enough for a step, ask whether the step is already a closed, finite mapping someone could write down on one page. If it is, a model is the expensive way to run a rule you already have — and if part of the step turns out not to be fully written down, that's worth knowing before you automate it with anything.

title: Where ambiguity is real and rules genuinely fail
description: Genuine ambiguity isn't an undocumented exception or messy data — it's a category whose boundary depends on information the input doesn't reliably contain, over a set of possible inputs no table could enumerate. That's where a rules engine structurally cannot follow, no matter how large you make it.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish genuine ambiguity from an undocumented exception or a data-quality problem
Explain why expanding a lookup table cannot resolve a genuinely ambiguous category

contentSections.title: The shipment the table can't see

contentSections.body: Corvid's freight classification lookup breaks on a real shipment: the commodity description reads "assorted promotional merchandise — mixed retail items, various weights." No row in the table matches cleanly, because the correct class depends on the density of the actual mix, which depends on which specific items are in the box, which the four-word description doesn't say. Two experienced classification clerks, given this exact shipment, ask different follow-up questions and could reasonably land on different classes — not because either one is careless, but because the description genuinely doesn't contain the fact the classification depends on.

This is a different failure from the previous lesson's hidden exception. There, the rule existed but wasn't written down anywhere the system could read it — a documentation problem with a documentation fix. Here, no amount of documentation would help, because the input space (arbitrary free-text descriptions of arbitrary mixed shipments) is effectively unbounded, and the correct answer depends on facts the description doesn't reliably carry at all.

The useful test: even an expert with unlimited time couldn't reduce this to a finite table, because the category boundary itself is fuzzy and depends on context the input doesn't contain. That's the shape of task judgment — human or model — exists for. It's also exactly the kind of task a model can be genuinely useful at, because a model pattern-matches against thousands of similar past cases instead of requiring the boundary to be written out in advance.

contentSections.scenario: A Corvid engineer's proposed fix for the "assorted promotional merchandise" classification failures: "Let's just add more rows to the lookup table — cover every commodity combination we've seen so far, and keep adding rows as new ones come in."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in treating this as a table-completeness problem?

options.label: The set of possible free-text descriptions of mixed shipments is effectively unbounded — no finite table can enumerate every combination, and the correct class for a genuinely novel mix depends on facts the short description doesn't contain at all
The table is fine, but the model reading it needs better training data
Clerks should stop accepting vague descriptions like "assorted merchandise" from shippers

feedback.unbounded-inputs: Right. Adding rows chases a moving, effectively infinite target. The tell isn't "we haven't seen this case before" — new cases showing up is normal even for a genuinely closed system. The tell is "no amount of additional rows would have prevented this specific case," because the correct answer depends on something outside the four corners of the input as given.
feedback.training-data: This treats the problem as a model-competence question, which misses the point entirely — the issue isn't that a model (or a table) hasn't seen enough examples yet, it's that the category itself has no closed definition for anything to be trained toward. A perfectly trained model still can't classify a mix it has no information about.
feedback.stricter-input: This is a real, worthwhile operational fix — requiring an itemized list would resolve many of these cases — but it sidesteps the actual question. Even with better descriptions, some shipments are legitimately mixed-item loads where the right class genuinely depends on judgment about the dominant category, and no table size fixes that residual on its own.

contentSections.mechanism: Genuine ambiguity is a category whose boundary depends on information the input doesn't reliably carry, over a set of possible inputs that can't be pre-enumerated. Adding rows to a table doesn't shrink that gap — it just adds more entries to a list that was never going to be complete. Recognizing this early is what stops a team from sinking months into an ever-growing rules table that keeps missing the next case exactly the same way it missed the last one.

contentSections.title: Ambiguity, or something that only looks like it

contentSections.body: Not everything that feels uncertain is genuine ambiguity in this sense. A rule someone never wrote down, or data that's often mistyped, both produce the same surface symptom — the system gets it wrong sometimes — but they need completely different fixes. Confusing the three is how a team ends up throwing a model at a documentation problem, or trying to write a bigger table around something no table was ever going to capture.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding, for five more Corvid step types, whether they show genuine ambiguity (a rules table structurally can't capture it), a hidden exception (a rule exists but isn't written down), or a data-quality problem (a different failure covered later in this track).
contentSections.question: Select every signal that specifically points at genuine ambiguity.

items.label: Two experienced staff, given the identical input, reasonably reach different correct-seeming answers
The correct answer depends on context that isn't present in the input at all, and can't reliably be added to it
New, previously-unseen cases keep showing up no matter how large the reference table gets
The rule exists and is written down, but nobody updated the system when it changed
The input data is often mistyped or incomplete
Staff have a shared informal rule of thumb they all apply consistently — they've just never written it down

explanation.reasonable-disagreement: Applicable. Genuine, reasonable disagreement among competent people on identical inputs is close to a definition of real ambiguity — there's no rule they're all failing to apply, because no single rule produces one right answer here.
explanation.context-not-present: Applicable. This is the mechanism itself: the boundary depends on a fact the input structurally doesn't carry, which is exactly what makes enumeration impossible.
explanation.novel-cases-persist: Applicable. If the miss rate on new cases doesn't shrink as the table grows, the table was never the bottleneck — the category's boundary is the bottleneck.
explanation.undocumented-change: Not applicable — this is last lesson's hidden-exception territory. A rule that exists but isn't reflected in the system is a maintenance and documentation problem, not ambiguity, and the fix is writing it down, not adding judgment.
explanation.mistyped-input: Not applicable. Messy input data is a different failure mode from ambiguity — the correct answer might be perfectly well-defined, it's just that the system can't see it because of a typo or missing field. That's a data problem, addressed later in this track.
explanation.unwritten-consensus: Not applicable, and this is the trap worth watching for. If staff genuinely converge on the same answer via a shared rule of thumb, that rule of thumb usually can be written down and turned into an actual rule — it's undocumented, not ambiguous. Mistaking the two means routing a task to a model or a person when a plain rule would have done the job for less.

contentSections.synthesis: The three signals that hold up all describe the same shape: real disagreement among experts, context the input doesn't carry, and a table that never converges no matter how large it gets. The three that don't are each a different, specific problem with a different, specific fix — and treating any of them as ambiguity means reaching for judgment (human or model) where a rule, a data-quality fix, or better documentation would have actually solved it.

contentSections.body: Genuine ambiguity isn't "we haven't written the rule down yet" and it isn't "the data is messy." It's a category whose boundary depends on information the input doesn't reliably carry, over a set of inputs no table could enumerate — and that's exactly the shape of task judgment, human or model, is actually for.

title: Cost, latency and debuggability as selection criteria
description: Once accuracy is roughly comparable across mechanisms, the choice between a fine-tuned model, a general-purpose model call, and a human clerk is made by three practical questions: what it costs at real volume, how fast the answer needs to come back, and whether a specific decision can be explained months later.

learningObjectives.text: Apply cost-at-volume, latency and debuggability as selection criteria once accuracy is comparable across mechanisms
Identify which of a step's requirements (real-time vs batch, auditable vs not) rules out a mechanism regardless of its accuracy

contentSections.title: Three questions that aren't about accuracy

contentSections.body: Corvid needs a mechanism for the genuinely ambiguous freight-class residual the last lesson identified — about 8% of shipments where the table has no matching row. A fine-tuned classifier, a general-purpose model call, and a human clerk could all plausibly reach similar accuracy on this population. The consultant's actual recommendation ends up hinging on none of that comparison. It hinges on cost per shipment at Corvid's real volume, whether the booking flow can wait a few seconds for an answer, and whether Corvid's compliance team can reconstruct why a specific classification was chosen if a customer disputes their freight bill six months later.

Three criteria worth applying once accuracy is roughly comparable across mechanisms:

**Cost at volume.** A per-call API cost that looks trivial in a demo can dwarf a human clerk's hourly wage once multiplied by real monthly volume — and can also be far more expensive than a small, purpose-built classifier trained only for this task, which typically costs a fraction of what a large general-purpose model charges per call.

**Latency.** Does the answer need to come back in under a second, blocking a live booking flow a customer is watching, or is next-business-day fine because the step runs in an overnight batch? A model call that takes several seconds is a non-issue in a batch job and a hard blocker in a live flow.

**Debuggability.** For a decision that might get disputed later — a customer's finance team challenging a freight bill, a regulator asking why a claim was denied — can you point at exactly why this specific decision was made: a rule, a table entry, a named clerk's note? Or only "the model produced this," with no reconstructable reasoning behind the specific call? Regulated or disputable decisions need the former.

contentSections.scenario: Corvid runs roughly 40,000 shipments a month through the classification residual. Before seeing the vendor invoice, make a guess.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many times more expensive is it to run this monthly volume through a general-purpose large-model API call per shipment, versus a small, purpose-built classifier trained just for freight classes?
contentSections.explanation: The actual comparison, once Corvid priced both out, came in at roughly 15x — the general-purpose model's per-call pricing reflects a model capable of far more than a fixed 18-category classification, and Corvid pays for that generality on every one of 40,000 calls whether it uses it or not. A small classifier built for exactly this task, on the same volume, costs a small fraction of that. This is the mechanism that makes cost-at-volume a real selection criterion rather than a rounding error: the gap only shows up once you multiply by actual monthly volume, not a demo's single test call.

contentSections.scenario: Corvid's real-time booking flow includes a credit-hold check that must return an answer in under a second, runs roughly 40,000 times a day, and — because customers sometimes dispute a denied booking with their finance department — needs to be explainable to someone outside Corvid months after the fact.
contentSections.question: Select every factor that should genuinely influence which mechanism handles this step.

items.label: The step must return an answer in under a second inside a live customer-facing flow
A specific decision may need to be explained to an external party (the customer's finance team) months later
The step runs 40,000 times a day, so a small per-call cost difference compounds into a material monthly figure
The vendor's demo of their classification tool looked impressive
The vendor is a well-known AI company
Staff currently doing this check by hand find it repetitive and want it automated

explanation.latency-requirement: Applicable. A hard sub-second requirement inside a live flow rules out any mechanism that can't reliably meet it — this is a real constraint on the mechanism choice, independent of accuracy.
explanation.explainability-need: Applicable. If a specific decision needs a reconstructable reason months later, that requirement rules out mechanisms that can't produce one — this is what debuggability actually means in practice.
explanation.cost-at-volume: Applicable. At 40,000 calls a day, a cost difference that looked negligible in a single test becomes a real line item — this is exactly the arithmetic the earlier prediction exercise made concrete.
explanation.vendor-demo-polish: Not applicable. A polished demo says nothing about cost at Corvid's volume, latency under real load, or whether a specific decision could be reconstructed later — none of the three criteria this lesson is built around.
explanation.vendor-reputation: Not applicable to this specific decision. A well-known vendor's product still has to clear the same three practical tests; brand name doesn't substitute for any of them.
explanation.staff-boredom: Not applicable as a mechanism-selection criterion, though it's a legitimate reason to prioritize automating this step at all. It says nothing about which mechanism should do the automating.

contentSections.synthesis: The three factors that hold up all map directly onto cost, latency and debuggability. The three that don't are real business considerations elsewhere in a project, but they don't test whether a mechanism can actually do this specific job under this specific step's real constraints.

contentSections.body: Once accuracy is roughly comparable across mechanisms, the decision is made by three practical questions: what it costs at real volume, how fast the answer needs to come back, and whether you can reconstruct why a specific decision was made months later. These are business questions, not model questions, and they often decide the mechanism before accuracy ever gets consulted.

title: Hybrid steps: rules first, model for the remainder
description: Most real automations aren't a single mechanism choice — they're a cascade, where rules resolve the closed majority for free, a model handles the genuinely ambiguous residual, and a human sees only the cases the model itself flags as uncertain or high-stakes.

learningObjectives.text: Design a cascading rules-then-model-then-human pipeline for a process with a mixed population of easy and ambiguous cases
Justify why each tier of a cascade should only see the subset of cases suited to it, rather than the full input population

contentSections.body: Corvid's final design for freight classification: apply the rules-table lookup first. It resolves roughly 85% of shipments instantly, for free, with a guaranteed-correct answer for anything matching a known commodity description. Only the unmatched ~15% — the genuinely ambiguous cases the earlier lesson identified — get routed to a classification model. And only the model's own low-confidence subset of that 15% gets routed further, to a human clerk. Three tiers, cascading, each one seeing only the cases the tier before it couldn't resolve.

This is the hybrid pattern: not "rules OR AI OR a human," but three tiers doing three different jobs on three different subsets of the same input stream. Rules handle the closed, enumerable population for near-zero cost and perfect auditability. A model handles the genuinely ambiguous residual, where pattern-matching across many past examples helps in a way no table could. A human sees only the model's own low-confidence cases, or anything crossing a stakes threshold regardless of confidence.

The benefits compound: cost drops sharply because most volume never reaches the expensive tier; auditability improves because rule-resolved cases are trivially explainable; and the model only has to be good at the harder subset it was actually built for, instead of being expected to perform uniformly well across an entire mixed population that includes the easy 85% it never needed to see in the first place.

contentSections.problem: Design the three-tier cascade for Corvid's freight classification step.

steps.label: Tier 1 — rule match attempt
steps.work: Every shipment's commodity description is checked against the published classification table first. If it matches a known row cleanly, the class is returned immediately.
steps.why: This resolves the closed, enumerable ~85% of shipments at near-zero cost, with an answer that's trivially auditable — the table row is the reason.

steps.label: Tier 2 — model for the unmatched residual
steps.work: Shipments that don't match any table row go to a classification model trained on past ambiguous-description cases and their resolved classes. The model returns a class and a confidence score.
steps.why: This is exactly the genuinely ambiguous population from the previous lesson — a rule can't be written for it, but pattern-matching across many similar past cases can produce a reasonable answer.

steps.label: Tier 3 — human review of low-confidence model output
steps.work: Of the model's output, anything below a set confidence threshold — or above a shipment-value threshold regardless of confidence — routes to a human classification clerk before the shipment books.
steps.why: The model's own uncertainty, plus a stakes threshold independent of it, decide which cases actually need a person. This keeps the clerk's workload to the genuinely hard fraction instead of every ambiguous case.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure: Corvid's damage-claim triage. Claims policy already sets a clean rule for small claims; a model could help with the mid-size population; and some claims should always reach a human adjuster regardless of what any model concludes.

blanks.prompt: What should Tier 1 (the rule) resolve, and why does it qualify as a closed mapping?
blanks.answer: claims under $50 are auto-approved per the existing policy threshold, because that threshold is already a fixed, written rule with no interpretation required
accept: claims under a fixed small-dollar threshold, auto-approved per written policy
blanks.why: A fixed dollar threshold already written into policy is exactly the closed-mapping case from the earlier lesson — nothing about it requires reading free text or weighing an exception.

blanks.prompt: What should Tier 2 (the model) handle, and what does it produce that Tier 3 needs?
blanks.answer: the mid-size claims that don't clear the auto-approve threshold, using pattern history to flag likely-valid versus likely-suspicious claims, producing a recommendation plus a confidence or risk score
accept: mid-size claims, flagged by pattern history, with a confidence score attached
blanks.why: This is the genuinely ambiguous residual — no clean rule distinguishes a valid claim from a suspicious one at this size, but pattern-matching against claim history can produce a useful signal, as long as it comes with a score Tier 3 can act on.

blanks.prompt: What should always route to Tier 3 (a human adjuster), regardless of what the model concludes?
blanks.answer: claims flagged low-confidence or suspicious by the model, and separately, every claim over a set dollar threshold (e.g. $5,000) regardless of the model's confidence
accept: low-confidence or suspicious claims, plus all high-dollar claims regardless of model confidence
blanks.why: This mirrors Tier 3 above: the model's own uncertainty routes hard cases to a person, and a stakes threshold set independently of confidence catches high-dollar claims even when the model is confident — because confidence and consequence are different things, and a wrong answer on a large claim costs more no matter how sure the model was.

faded.procedure: For each step type: what closed rule can Tier 1 resolve outright? What genuinely ambiguous residual is left for Tier 2, and what score does it need to hand off? And what combination of low model confidence and high stakes should always land on Tier 3, independent of how well the model is generally performing?

contentSections.body: A cascade only works if its boundaries are set on purpose. "Send everything to the model and see what happens" isn't a hybrid design — it's a single mechanism wearing three tiers as a label. The two boundaries that actually need deciding, in writing, before a cascade ships: what exactly counts as a rule match at Tier 1 (loose enough to catch real matches, strict enough not to silently absorb an ambiguous case), and what confidence threshold plus what stakes threshold routes to Tier 3. Both should be revisited on a schedule as real volume passes through, not set once and forgotten.

Most real automations aren't a single mechanism choice — they're a cascade, where each tier only sees the cases the tier before it couldn't resolve. Design the boundaries deliberately, in writing, instead of defaulting to "send everything to the model and hope."

title: Steps that must stay human, and how to say why
description: Some mechanism-selection decisions should never resolve to "let the best-performing option run unsupervised," no matter how good that option's average accuracy gets — because what's really being decided is what a wrong answer costs on the specific case, and who is accountable for it.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a step whose oversight requirement should scale with accuracy from one whose oversight requirement is set by stakes, independent of accuracy
Respond to a stakeholder's accuracy-based argument for removing a human step without conceding a category-based decision it doesn't actually touch

contentSections.title: "If it's right 97% of the time, why review it?"

contentSections.body: Corvid's damage-claim design routes claims over $5,000 to a human adjuster regardless of what the model recommends — even once the model has an excellent track record on that population. The CFO pushes back: "If the model's right 97% of the time on claims this size, why not let it decide and only review the ones it flags as uncertain?" This isn't a capability question. It's the mechanism-selection version of a distinction this track has drawn before: some decisions need a human not because no mechanism reaches adequate average accuracy, but because of what's riding on the specific case it gets wrong.

The tell isn't "how often is it wrong" — it's "what happens, and who is accountable, on the specific cases it's wrong about, and does that consequence scale with the case's stakes rather than the mechanism's average performance." A 97%-accurate model on $5,000+ claims still gets roughly 1 in 33 of those large claims wrong. If nobody is positioned to catch which one, the business is accepting a fixed rate of large, unreviewed, unaccountable errors — and that rate doesn't fall as the model improves, because the review requirement was never about the model's accuracy to begin with. It was about the fact that a wrong decision on a claim this size, litigation exposure, regulatory scrutiny, or a long-standing carrier relationship carries a cost that a rule or model has no visibility into and no accountability for.

This is a genuinely different argument from "the model isn't accurate enough," and a client who has invested in a strong accuracy number will keep answering the accuracy argument by promising a better one. The stakes-based argument survives that, because a better model doesn't change what a wrong decision on a $5,000 claim costs, or who has to answer for it.

contentSections.title: The CFO wants the $5,000 threshold removed
contentSections.opening: Corvid's damage-claim model has run for six months with a 97% agreement rate with what a human adjuster would have decided, on claims over $5,000. The CFO emails: "Given these numbers, can we just let the model decide these outright and only review what it flags as low-confidence?"

reply.situation: You need to respond before the next finance review.
reply.question: What's the right first move?

choices.label: Agree — a 97% agreement rate over six months is strong evidence the review step can be relaxed to confidence-based only
choices.consequence: This treats the review step as if it existed to compensate for the model's accuracy, and concedes that a strong number is enough to remove it. It wasn't there for that reason — it was there because of what a wrong decision on a claim this size costs, and that hasn't moved.

choices.label: Reply that the threshold is policy and isn't up for discussion
choices.consequence: This is true but unhelpful — it gives the CFO no reason, which means the same request resurfaces at the next strong quarter, and it reads as reflexive rather than reasoned to someone genuinely trying to reduce review overhead.

choices.label: Separate two questions: is the 97% figure genuinely strong evidence (worth checking properly), and does that figure change why claims over $5,000 get reviewed in the first place (it doesn't, and here's why)
choices.consequence: You've split the two things the CFO's email bundled together — a real, checkable data point about model performance, and a category-based policy decision that isn't actually about model performance at all.

explain.situation: You confirm the 97% figure is real and well-measured. It's genuinely good news about the model's performance on this population.
explain.question: How do you close this out with the CFO?

choices.label: Credit the number honestly, then explain that the review threshold was never set by accuracy — it exists because a wrong decision on a claim this size can mean litigation exposure or a damaged carrier relationship that a model has no visibility into, and 1 in 33 large claims going unreviewed at 97% is still a real, unaccountable exposure at this volume
choices.consequence: The CFO gets a real answer: the number is good, the threshold stays for a different, durable reason, and the reasoning would hold even if the model reached 99%.

choices.label: Say the model "still needs more testing" before the threshold could change
choices.consequence: This implies the threshold is provisional and waiting on a better number — which sets up the exact same conversation again next quarter, because it never named the actual, stakes-based reason the review exists.

conceded.summary: A stakes-based review requirement got removed on an accuracy argument. If this ships, roughly 1 in 33 large claims — the exact population where a wrong call is most expensive — now resolves with no one positioned to catch it.
conceded.lesson: A strong accuracy number answers "is the model good" — it doesn't answer "what should happen when it's wrong on an expensive case," and conflating the two removes a safeguard that was never about accuracy in the first place.

unexplained.summary: The immediate request is turned down, but the CFO never gets the actual reason. The same request returns next quarter with an even better number attached, because nothing durable was explained this time.
unexplained.lesson: Defending a stakes-based threshold requires naming the stakes explicitly — what a wrong decision costs and who answers for it — not just asserting that the policy exists.

durable.summary: The CFO leaves with two separate, true things: the model's performance is genuinely strong, and the review threshold exists for a reason that doesn't move when the model's number does. The next strong quarter, this conversation doesn't have to happen again.
durable.lesson: The mechanism-selection question for high-stakes steps isn't "is this good enough on average" — it's "what does a wrong answer cost on this specific case, and who is accountable for it." Naming that clearly, separate from crediting real accuracy gains, is what makes the answer durable.

contentSections.body: For some decisions, the mechanism-selection question isn't "is this good enough on average" — it's "what does a wrong answer cost on the specific case, and who is accountable for it." Those steps stay human regardless of how the average performance number reads, and saying so clearly, with the reason named, is part of the deliverable.

Distinguish a defensible mechanism assignment from one that defaults to whichever option is newest
