If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Produce a Mechanism Map for a Full Process
description: Decompose a real process into its steps, assign each one a mechanism — rule, model, human, or a cascade — and write a defensible justification for every step you'd hand to AI.

learningObjectives.text: Decompose a real process into steps and assign each a defensible mechanism
Justify a mechanism assignment using closed-mapping, ambiguity, and cost/latency/debuggability reasoning rather than intuition

contentSections.body: Pick a real process you know — from your own work, a client's, or one you can research concretely enough to reason about honestly. You're going to break it into its actual steps and decide, step by step, what mechanism should run each one — and for every step you assign to AI, write down exactly why, using this module's tests rather than a gut feeling.

contentSections.title: Your mechanism map
contentSections.brief: Choose one real, multi-step process — a real workflow you know well enough to describe accurately, not a hypothetical. You'll decompose it, assign a mechanism to each step, and justify every AI assignment against this module's criteria.
contentSections.deliverable: A step-by-step mechanism assignment (rule / model / human / cascade) for a full process, with a written justification for every step assigned to AI, referencing the closed-mapping test, the ambiguity test, or the cost/latency/debuggability criteria.

stages.title: Decompose the process into real steps
stages.instructions: Write out the process as a sequence of individual steps — not as one named process, but as the actual decisions and actions it contains, the way the earlier lessons broke Corvid's freight-class check apart from its credit-hold check. Aim for 5-8 distinct steps.
stages.checkpoint: You have a numbered list of 5-8 real steps, each one a single decision or action, not a bundle of several.

stages.title: Apply the closed-mapping and ambiguity tests to each step
stages.instructions: For each step, ask: is the mapping from input to output already fully written down somewhere (closed — a rule candidate), or does the correct answer depend on context the input doesn't reliably carry (genuinely ambiguous — a model or human candidate)? Note your answer and reasoning for each step.
stages.checkpoint: Every step has a closed-or-ambiguous call with a one-sentence reason, not just a label.

stages.title: Assign a mechanism and apply cost/latency/debuggability to the ambiguous steps
stages.instructions: For every step you called genuinely ambiguous, decide model, human, or a rules-then-model-then-human cascade. Justify the choice using cost at your process's real (or realistic estimated) volume, latency requirements, and whether a specific decision would need to be explained later.
stages.checkpoint: Every ambiguous step has a mechanism assignment and a justification that names at least one of cost, latency, or debuggability specifically — not a generic "AI would be good at this."

stages.title: Write the final mechanism map and self-check against the rubric
stages.instructions: Assemble the full step-by-step map: step, mechanism, justification. Read back through it against the rubric below before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: The map covers every step from stage 1, and every AI-assigned step has a justification a colleague could evaluate without asking you a follow-up question.

rubric.criterion: The process is broken into real, distinct steps, not one bundled description
rubric.meets: 5-8 steps, each a single decision or action a mechanism could be assigned to individually.

rubric.criterion: Every step has a closed-mapping or genuine-ambiguity call with real reasoning
rubric.meets: The reasoning references whether the mapping is already fully written down or depends on context the input doesn't carry — not just a label.

rubric.criterion: Rule-assigned steps are genuinely closed
rubric.meets: Any step assigned to a plain rule could actually be expressed as a formula or a short table, per this module's test.

rubric.criterion: AI-assigned steps are justified with cost, latency, or debuggability specifically
rubric.meets: Each justification names at least one concrete factor — a realistic volume figure, a real-time requirement, or a need to explain a specific decision later — not a generic capability claim.

rubric.criterion: At least one step, if genuinely warranted by the process, stays human regardless of mechanism accuracy
rubric.meets: If the process contains a high-stakes decision, the map names it and states the stakes-based reason, separate from any accuracy argument.

rubric.criterion: A colleague could implement from this map without asking a follow-up question
rubric.meets: Each row states the step, the mechanism, and the specific reason — nothing left implied.

contentSections.body: A mechanism map that just says "AI" next to every non-trivial step hasn't actually decided anything. The justification per step — closed or ambiguous, and why this specific mechanism at this specific cost, latency, and stakes — is the actual deliverable.

title: Checkpoint — Rules, AI, or a Person
description: Ten questions, six from this module and four from the previous one. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's mechanism-selection distinctions, and the previous module's capability distinctions, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Rules, AI, or a Person

questions.from: This module — Rules, AI, or a Person
questions.prompt: What makes a process step a genuinely closed mapping that never needed a model?

options.label: The step runs very frequently
The complete mapping from input to one correct output is already written down somewhere, and two competent people would always agree
The AI version of it currently gets the right answer almost all the time

questions.explanation: Corvid's fuel surcharge calculation was the clean case: a formula against two known numbers, with nothing left to interpret. Volume and current AI accuracy were both shown to be the wrong signals to trust.

questions.from: This module — Rules, AI, or a Person
questions.prompt: A step "looks" mechanical but has an unrecorded manual override path for certain accounts. What kind of problem is this, and what's the fix?

options.label: Genuine ambiguity — no rule could ever capture it, so it needs a model
A hidden exception — the rule exists but isn't written down anywhere the system can read it, so the fix is documenting it, not automating around it
A data-quality problem that needs cleaner input

questions.explanation: Corvid's credit-hold check had exactly this shape — a threshold rule with an unrecorded manual override for legacy accounts. That's a documentation gap, not evidence the step needs judgment.

questions.from: This module — Rules, AI, or a Person
questions.prompt: Why can't a bigger lookup table fix Corvid's "assorted promotional merchandise" classification failures?

options.label: The table just needs to be updated more frequently
The set of possible free-text descriptions is effectively unbounded, and the correct class depends on facts the short description doesn't contain at all
The model reading the table needs better training data

questions.explanation: Genuine ambiguity is defined by the input not reliably carrying the fact the correct answer depends on — no amount of additional rows fixes that, because the gap isn't in the table's size.

questions.from: This module — Rules, AI, or a Person
questions.prompt: Once accuracy is roughly comparable across mechanisms, what actually decides which one to use?

options.label: Whichever mechanism is the newest technology
Cost at real volume, latency requirements, and whether a specific decision needs to be explainable later
Whichever vendor has the best reputation

questions.explanation: Corvid's classification-residual decision hinged on exactly these three practical questions once accuracy stopped being the differentiator — a 15x cost gap at real volume, a latency requirement, and a need to reconstruct a disputed decision months later.

questions.from: This module — Rules, AI, or a Person
questions.prompt: In a rules-then-model-then-human cascade, what should each tier actually see?

options.label: Every tier sees the full input population, for redundancy

Each tier sees only the subset the tier before it couldn't resolve — rules take the closed majority, the model takes the genuinely ambiguous residual, a human takes the model's own low-confidence or high-stakes cases
The model should always see everything first, with rules only as a final fallback

questions.explanation: Corvid's freight-class cascade resolved ~85% at the rule tier for free, sent only the genuinely ambiguous ~15% to the model, and only the model's own low-confidence subset of that to a human — each tier doing the job it's actually suited to.

questions.from: This module — Rules, AI, or a Person
questions.prompt: Corvid's CFO argues a 97%-accurate model should be allowed to decide large damage claims unsupervised. What's the strongest response?

options.label: Agree — 97% is strong evidence the review step can be relaxed
The review threshold was never set by accuracy — it exists because of what a wrong decision on a claim this size costs and who is accountable for it, and that reasoning doesn't change even at 99%
Refuse to discuss it because it's policy

questions.explanation: This is the case-sim's durable ending: crediting the real accuracy number honestly while explaining that the threshold is stakes-based, not accuracy-based — a distinction that survives even a better model.

questions.from: Previous module — What These Systems Can Actually Do
questions.prompt: What is a language model actually doing when it produces an answer?

options.label: Reading the input and verifying its conclusion against what it knows to be true
Predicting the statistically likely next text given the input and its training patterns — which can be right without ever having been verified
Looking up the answer in a database of stored, confirmed facts

questions.explanation: Prediction from pattern, conditioned on the actual input — the Bramwell & Cho lease example showed this can be correct with no verification step in the mechanism at all.

questions.from: Previous module — What These Systems Can Actually Do
questions.prompt: Why is the "unreliable in a way you won't notice" failure category the most dangerous one?

options.label: It happens more often than other failure types
It reads exactly as fluent and confident as a correct answer, so it passes any review that only checks whether output looks right
It only affects low-stakes tasks

questions.explanation: Larkspur's dropped-dosage summary was perfectly formatted and read clearly — nothing about it would trip a review process checking readability instead of source accuracy.

questions.from: Previous module — What These Systems Can Actually Do
questions.prompt: Which of the four task categories (classification, extraction, drafting, deciding) carries the highest stakes, and why?

options.label: Classification, because it's used most often
Deciding, because it's the only one where the AI's output takes effect directly, with no human step positioned to catch an error before it happens
Drafting, because generated text is unpredictable

questions.explanation: The auto-resubmit example showed a deciding task inherits any upstream error and acts on it with nobody positioned to catch it — the same reasoning behind this module's stakes-based human-review threshold.

questions.from: Previous module — What These Systems Can Actually Do
questions.prompt: A vendor claims "96% accuracy" for a tool. What does that headline number, on its own, fail to tell you?

options.label: Nothing — a well-measured aggregate number is sufficient on its own
Whether the errors are evenly distributed or concentrated in a specific condition or subgroup that matters to your client
The name of the vendor's test set

questions.explanation: The 96% headline hid a 78% figure on exactly the condition Larkspur actually recorded in — an aggregate can average a strong majority condition with a weak minority one and still look respectable.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Decisions that affect somebody's money, health or record
description: A specific class of decision deserves a named human owner regardless of how good the automation gets: one that changes what someone is owed, what care they receive, or what their permanent record says about them.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a decision as belonging to the money/health/record class that warrants explicit human ownership
Distinguish this class from a step that's merely high-volume or currently error-prone

contentSections.body: Halsey Tenant Screening runs background checks for landlords: criminal record matches, eviction history, credit summary. Its automated risk score now flags applicants directly — a score above a threshold produces an auto-decline that the landlord's leasing software sends out with no person at Halsey ever looking at the specific file. One applicant, Marcus Webb, gets declined over a criminal record that turns out to belong to a different Marcus Webb, born nine years apart, in a different state. The match was statistically reasonable — common name, close birth year — and it was also wrong, and it cost a specific person a specific apartment, with nobody at Halsey positioned to have caught it before it went out.

This case sits in a specific class this lesson names directly: a decision that changes what someone is owed, what care they receive, or what their permanent record says about them. Not every automatable step belongs to this class — the freight-classification and fuel-surcharge examples from the previous module don't touch anyone's money, health, or record in this sense. A tenant screening decision does: it can cost someone housing, and it can attach a specific claim ("this record belongs to you") to their name that follows them to the next landlord too.

The test isn't how good the automation's average accuracy is — Halsey's matching algorithm might be genuinely excellent on average. The test is whether a wrong decision in this class has a consequence that lands on a specific person, is hard to reverse once it's acted on, and touches money, health, or a record that outlives this one transaction. When a step clears that bar, it needs a named human owner, not just a confidence threshold.

contentSections.scenario: Halsey runs several automated steps: (1) auto-populating a report template with the applicant's name, address history and requested unit from the landlord's form; (2) matching a criminal record database entry to the applicant by name, birth date and location; (3) formatting the final PDF report with Halsey's letterhead and page numbers; (4) flagging an applicant's income as insufficient to meet a landlord's 3x-rent requirement, based on submitted pay stubs.
contentSections.question: Which of these four steps most clearly belongs in the money/health/record class this lesson defines — the class that needs a named human owner regardless of the algorithm's average accuracy?

options.label: Step 2 — matching a criminal record to the applicant
Step 3 — formatting the final PDF report
Step 1 — auto-populating the report template

feedback.step2-match: Right. A wrong match attaches a criminal record to the wrong person's name, can cost them housing, and — because Halsey's report may be shared with other landlords or resold — the wrong attribution can outlive this one application. That's exactly the class this lesson names: a consequence that's hard to reverse and attaches to a specific person's record.
feedback.step3-format: This is purely cosmetic — page numbers and letterhead don't change what the report says about anyone. A wrong outcome here (a typo in the header) is trivially reversible and touches nobody's money, health or record.
feedback.step1-populate: This copies fields the applicant already provided, without adding any new claim about them — if the address is wrong, it's wrong because the applicant's own form was wrong, and it doesn't attach a new, disputable fact like a record match does. It's a real step to get right, but it isn't a judgment call in this lesson's sense.

contentSections.concept: The class this lesson defines isn't "anything involving personal data" or "anything customer-facing" — it's specifically a decision that changes what someone is owed, what care they receive, or what their permanent record says, in a way that's hard to reverse and can outlive the immediate transaction. Formatting and field-copying don't clear that bar even though they touch the same applicant's data. A record match does, because being wrongly linked to someone else's criminal history is exactly the kind of harm that doesn't undo itself when the mistake is later found.

contentSections.body: It's tempting to over-apply this class to anything that feels important, which dilutes it until it stops being useful for deciding where a human owner is actually required. The class is specifically about consequences to a person — money, health, record — not about how central a step is to the business, how much revenue it touches, or how embarrassing a mistake would be internally.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding, for five more Halsey process steps, whether each belongs in the money/health/record class that needs a named human owner.
contentSections.question: Select every step that genuinely belongs in this class.

items.label: Matching an eviction filing to an applicant, which can independently disqualify them from a lease
Flagging an applicant's income as insufficient, which can lead to an automatic denial under a landlord's policy
Deciding how to resolve an applicant's dispute that a matched record isn't theirs
The step runs on every one of Halsey's several thousand monthly reports
The step is central to Halsey's business model and revenue
A mistake here would be embarrassing if a client noticed it

explanation.eviction-match: Applicable. Same shape as the criminal-record match: a specific fact gets attached to a specific applicant, it can independently disqualify them from housing, and it's hard to reverse once a landlord has already acted on it.
explanation.income-flag: Applicable. This directly changes what someone is offered — a home — based on a judgment about their finances, with a consequence that lands on them specifically and isn't easily undone once a landlord has denied the application on it.
explanation.dispute-resolution: Applicable, and arguably the clearest case: this is the step where an applicant is actively asserting the automation got their record wrong. Automating away the resolution of that specific dispute removes the one place the original error could be caught and corrected.
explanation.high-volume: Not applicable as membership in this class. Volume is a reason to care about a step's cost and throughput — it says nothing about whether a wrong decision on any single case harms a specific person's money, health, or record.
explanation.revenue-critical: Not applicable. How central a step is to the business model is a different axis entirely from whether a wrong decision harms a person in this specific way — a step can be revenue-critical and purely cosmetic (like report formatting) at the same time.
explanation.internally-embarrassing: Not applicable. Internal embarrassment is about Halsey's reputation with a client, not about consequence to the applicant whose record is being processed — those can align, but this signal alone doesn't establish the class membership this lesson is testing for.

contentSections.synthesis: The three that qualify all share the same shape: a specific consequence, to a specific person, that's hard to reverse and touches their money, health, or record. The three that don't are all real business concerns — worth caring about for other reasons — but they don't answer the question this lesson asks, which is about harm to the person the decision is about, not about the business making it.

contentSections.body: A decision earns a named human owner not because it's important to the business, high-volume, or currently error-prone — but because a wrong call changes what someone is owed, what care they receive, or what their record says, in a way that's hard to reverse once it's acted on.

title: Accountability that can't be delegated to a system
description: "The system decided" is not an accepted answer when a specific person disputes a specific decision — accountability has to sit with a named role, and that requirement doesn't disappear just because the system is accurate.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an automated system cannot itself be the accountable party for a disputed decision
Identify what a named accountable role needs in order to actually answer for a decision, not just be nominally attached to it

contentSections.body: Marcus Webb, wrongly declined over a mismatched criminal record, calls Halsey to dispute it. The support rep who takes the call checks the system and reports back: "Our matching algorithm flagged this as a 96% confidence match, and the algorithm is generally very reliable, so there's not much I can do." This is, functionally, the sentence "the system decided," said out loud to someone whose apartment application it just cost. It isn't an answer, because a system isn't a party that can be held accountable for anything — it has no job to be fired from, no license to lose, no obligation it can be shown to have failed. Somebody at Halsey has to be the party who actually answers for this specific decision, and right now nobody is.

Accountability that can't be delegated to a system means: for any decision in the money/health/record class, there has to be a named human role whose job includes actually answering for a specific instance of that decision — not a general statement that "the algorithm is usually right," but a person who can look at this specific case, this specific match, and either defend it or correct it.

This is a different requirement from accuracy. A highly accurate system still needs this, because accuracy is a statement about the population of decisions, and accountability is about the one decision in front of you right now, which either was or wasn't correct regardless of what the population-level number says. A named accountable role needs three things to actually function, not just exist on an org chart: **visibility** into the specific case being disputed (not just the system's summary output), **authority** to reverse or correct the decision, and **a real obligation** to respond — a role that exists on paper but has no time budgeted for it, or no actual power to change the outcome, isn't accountability, it's a title.

contentSections.scenario: Halsey's revised process after the Marcus Webb complaint: disputes are now routed to a "Quality Assurance" inbox. The QA team's stated job is to "review flagged disputes," but they have no access to the underlying record-matching database — only the same summary PDF the landlord received — and no documented authority to overturn a landlord's decision once it's been sent.
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in calling this a fix for the accountability gap?

options.label: The QA team lacks both the visibility to actually re-examine the underlying match and the authority to correct it — the role exists on paper without the two things that would let it function
The team should be called something other than "Quality Assurance"
The process is too slow to be useful

feedback.no-authority-visibility: Right. A named role only provides real accountability if it can actually see enough to evaluate the disputed decision and actually has the power to change the outcome. Without database access, the QA team is reviewing the same summary the algorithm produced, which can't reveal whether the algorithm's own match was wrong. Without documented authority to overturn a decision, even a QA reviewer who correctly spots the error has no path to fix it.
feedback.wrong-team-name: The name isn't the problem — a differently-named team with the same access limitations and lack of authority would fail in exactly the same way. This distracts from the actual structural gap.
feedback.too-slow: Speed is a real, separate concern worth raising, but it isn't the flaw this scenario is built to surface. A QA team that responded instantly, with the same lack of visibility and authority, would still be unable to actually catch or correct the Marcus Webb case.

contentSections.mechanism: A named role becomes real accountability only when it has visibility into the specific decision being questioned and the authority to change it. Naming a team without giving it either is decorative — it produces the appearance of a review step without the capability that makes a review step actually able to catch and correct an error.

contentSections.body: "The system decided" is never an acceptable answer to a specific person disputing a specific decision, and naming a team to "handle it" only counts as accountability if that team can actually see the disputed case and actually has the power to change the outcome.

title: Automation bias: humans stop checking what's usually right
description: A reviewer who's watched an automated system be right hundreds of times in a row stops actually checking, even while formally still "reviewing" every case — and the tell isn't laziness, it's a predictable response to a system that's genuinely good most of the time.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the conditions that predictably produce automation bias in a human reviewer
Recognize the behavioral symptoms of automation bias in a review process, distinct from a reviewer simply being careless

contentSections.body: After the Marcus Webb incident, Halsey adds a human review step: every record match above the auto-decline threshold gets a two-minute look from a screening analyst before the report goes out. Six months in, an audit finds the analysts are approving 99.4% of flagged matches — almost exactly the algorithm's own historical accuracy rate — and the average time spent per review has dropped to eleven seconds. Nobody told the analysts to stop checking. They didn't get lazier as people. What happened is a well-documented, predictable response to watching a system be right almost every single time: the checking behavior itself quietly stopped costing enough attention to be worth doing.

Automation bias is the tendency to over-trust an automated system's output specifically because it has usually been right — not a character flaw, but a predictable response to specific conditions: high (but not perfect) accuracy, a repetitive task, and time or volume pressure. All three were present at Halsey: the matching algorithm really is accurate most of the time, analysts see dozens of matches a day, and eleven seconds per case is what a caseload of that size under a normal shift actually allows once the checking stops feeling necessary.

The symptoms are specific and worth naming, because they let you catch this without waiting for another wrongful denial: review time drops toward a floor that couldn't possibly include re-examining the underlying evidence; the override rate converges toward zero and stays there even as case volume and complexity vary; and reviewers, when asked, describe their own process as "the algorithm is really good, so I mostly just confirm it" — a description of trust replacing verification, said without anyone noticing the substitution happened.

contentSections.scenario: You're auditing Halsey's review process for signs of automation bias, six months after the human-review step was introduced.
contentSections.question: Select every finding that's a genuine symptom of automation bias, as opposed to something that just sounds concerning on its own.

items.label: Average review time has dropped to eleven seconds, well below what re-examining the underlying match evidence would plausibly take
The override rate has converged to almost exactly the algorithm's own historical accuracy rate and stayed flat regardless of case complexity
Analysts describe their process as "I mostly just confirm it, since the algorithm's really good"
Analysts review dozens of cases a day
The underlying matching algorithm genuinely is accurate most of the time
Two analysts left the screening team this quarter

explanation.time-floor: Applicable. Time spent is a direct, measurable proxy for whether verification is actually happening — eleven seconds isn't enough to re-examine a record match, so the review step has structurally stopped doing the thing it exists to do.
explanation.override-near-zero: Applicable, especially combined with flatness across complexity — a genuinely engaged reviewer should override more often on harder cases, not maintain a constant rate regardless of how ambiguous the underlying match is.
explanation.self-description: Applicable, and often the clearest signal, because it names the mechanism directly: trust in the algorithm's general track record has replaced verification of the specific case in front of them.
explanation.high-volume-alone: Not applicable by itself — high volume is one of the three conditions that predictably produce automation bias, but it isn't evidence the bias has actually occurred. A high-volume reviewer who still spends real time per case and overrides at a rate that tracks complexity is not exhibiting automation bias, just doing a high-volume job.
explanation.algorithm-accurate: Not applicable by itself, for the same reason — high accuracy is one of the preconditions for automation bias to develop, but the algorithm being accurate is not itself evidence the human review step has stopped functioning. It's a risk factor, not a symptom.
explanation.staff-turnover: Not applicable. Turnover is a real HR data point but isn't a symptom of automation bias specifically — it could reflect any number of unrelated causes and doesn't speak to whether the remaining or departed staff were actually verifying cases.

contentSections.synthesis: The three genuine symptoms are all behavioral evidence that checking has stopped happening in practice: time spent, an override rate that doesn't track difficulty, and reviewers' own account of relying on trust rather than verification. The three non-symptoms are either preconditions that make bias more likely (accuracy, volume) or unrelated data points (turnover) — real to track for other reasons, but they don't tell you whether the bias has actually set in.

contentSections.title: Why the accurate algorithm made this worse, not better

contentSections.code:
Halsey's response memo after the audit:

"Given that the algorithm's accuracy has been independently validated at over 99%, and analyst override rates track that figure closely, we're confident the human review step is functioning as intended and no changes are needed."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in using the override rate matching the algorithm's accuracy as evidence the review step is working?

options.label: An override rate that matches the algorithm's own accuracy is exactly what you'd expect from a reviewer who has stopped independently checking and is just agreeing with the algorithm by default — it's consistent with the review working, and equally consistent with automation bias having fully set in
Accuracy should be measured differently
The 99% validation figure itself is untrustworthy

feedback.circular: Right. This is the trap: if analysts are genuinely re-verifying each case, you'd expect their override rate to roughly track the algorithm's error rate. But if analysts have stopped verifying and are simply rubber-stamping the algorithm's output, you'd see the exact same number, because the "override rate" would just be measuring the algorithm's own accuracy relabeled as human judgment. The metric can't distinguish the two explanations, which is exactly why it shouldn't be treated as reassuring on its own.
feedback.wrong-metric: The measurement method isn't the core issue here — the problem is that this particular metric, however it's measured, is structurally unable to distinguish real verification from rubber-stamping.
feedback.not-independent: Nothing in the scenario suggests the 99% figure itself is unreliable — the flaw is in what conclusion gets drawn from the override rate matching it, not in the underlying accuracy measurement.

contentSections.flawExplanation: An override rate near the algorithm's own accuracy rate is ambiguous evidence by construction — it's the expected outcome under both "the review step works" and "the review step has collapsed into automation bias." A metric that can't tell those two situations apart shouldn't be cited as proof the review step is functioning; you need the direct evidence from the earlier exercise instead — time spent per case, and whether override rate tracks case complexity rather than just tracking the algorithm's aggregate performance.

contentSections.body: Automation bias isn't a character flaw in a careless reviewer — it's a predictable response to a genuinely accurate system, a repetitive task, and volume pressure. It shows up as review time collapsing toward a floor, an override rate that stops tracking case difficulty, and reviewers describing their own process as trust rather than verification — and a high accuracy number is not, on its own, evidence the review step is still working.

title: Meaningful review versus rubber-stamping
description: A review step that nominally exists but requires no real friction to pass isn't oversight — it's a rubber stamp with an extra click. Meaningful review has to make skipping the actual check harder than doing it.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish design features that produce meaningful review from ones that produce a rubber stamp with an added step
Propose a specific design change that converts a rubber-stamp review into one that actually requires looking

contentSections.body: Halsey's original review screen showed analysts a single "Approve match" button, pre-selected, with the underlying evidence (the two names, birth dates, addresses side by side) available only behind a separate "view details" link most analysts, under time pressure, never clicked. Clicking Approve took one motion. Actually comparing the details took a genuine, separate action nobody was required to take. The screen technically had a human in the loop. It was designed, probably without anyone intending it, to make the path of least resistance identical to not reviewing anything at all.

Meaningful review and rubber-stamping can look identical from the outside — both produce a human clicking "approve" on most cases. The difference is in what the interface and the incentives actually require before that click is possible.

A few concrete design features separate the two: **the comparison data is shown by default**, not hidden behind an extra click nobody has time for; **approving requires an action distinct from doing nothing**, so a reviewer can't advance the queue without registering a decision (a pre-selected default button fails this test even if it technically requires a click); **the review has a genuine cost to skipping** — either logged time-on-case that's visible to a manager, or a required field the reviewer has to fill in that can't be satisfied with a copy-pasted non-answer; and **disagreement is at least as easy as agreement** — if overriding the algorithm takes five extra steps and approving takes one, the interface itself is quietly training reviewers toward automation bias regardless of anyone's intent.

contentSections.intro: Redesign Halsey's review screen so that approving a flagged match actually requires looking at it. Three decisions.

fields.prompt: What should the review screen show by default, before any click?

options.label: A single pre-selected "Approve" button, with the comparison data available behind a "view details" link
The applicant's and the matched record's names, birth dates and locations shown side by side, with no pre-selected action
Just the algorithm's confidence score and a summary sentence

feedback.visible-comparison: Right. This is the same fix from an earlier lesson's silent-failure discussion, applied here: a reviewer can only meaningfully check something they can actually see without extra effort. Showing the comparison by default removes the one-click path around it.
feedback.hidden-details: This is the original design that failed — putting the actual evidence behind an optional link means most reviewers, under time pressure, never see the thing they're supposed to be reviewing.
feedback.score-only: A confidence score is a summary of the algorithm's own judgment, not independent evidence a human can check it against — showing only the score gives the reviewer nothing to verify, only something to trust.

fields.prompt: What should it take to approve a match?

options.label: A pre-selected default the reviewer can advance past without changing anything
An explicit action — clicking a specific 'Confirm match' control that isn't pre-selected — so advancing the queue requires registering a real decision
Automatic approval after a fixed number of seconds if no action is taken

feedback.explicit-confirm: Right. Requiring an explicit, non-default action closes the path where a reviewer can advance the queue without making any decision at all — it doesn't guarantee real scrutiny, but it removes the version of the interface that made non-review literally the default outcome.
feedback.default-preselected: This is exactly the original flaw. A pre-selected default means the reviewer's "decision" can be made by doing nothing, which is functionally identical to no review happening.
feedback.auto-timeout: This is worse than the original design, not better — it converts inaction into approval automatically, actively rewarding a reviewer for not engaging rather than merely failing to require engagement.

fields.prompt: How much harder should overriding the algorithm's match be, relative to approving it?

options.label: Considerably harder — overriding should require a written justification and a supervisor sign-off, while approving stays a single click
Roughly the same amount of friction as approving — both require the reviewer to register the decision and, for override, a one-line reason
Overriding should be impossible without escalating to a manager first, to prevent inconsistent decisions

feedback.similar-friction: Right. If disagreeing with the algorithm takes meaningfully more effort than agreeing with it, the interface itself nudges every borderline case toward approval regardless of what the reviewer actually thinks — quietly manufacturing the same automation-bias pattern this module is trying to prevent. A one-line reason on override is a reasonable, light-touch accountability record, not a barrier.
feedback.much-harder: This directly reproduces the incentive structure that caused the original failure — making disagreement expensive relative to agreement predictably suppresses disagreement, whether or not the reviewer actually believes the match is wrong.
feedback.escalation-required: Requiring a manager for every override adds real delay and workload for a step meant to run per-case, and it doesn't address the actual asymmetry problem — it just moves the friction rather than removing it.

contentSections.synthesis: A review step becomes meaningful through specific, checkable design choices: the evidence is visible without extra effort, approving requires a genuine action rather than inaction, and disagreeing is no harder than agreeing. None of these guarantee a reviewer will always catch a wrong match — but a screen missing any of them guarantees, structurally, that most reviewers eventually won't.

contentSections.body: A review step that technically has a human clicking "approve" isn't automatically meaningful oversight. It's meaningful when the evidence is visible by default, approving requires a real action, and disagreeing costs no more effort than agreeing — remove any one of those and the interface itself starts manufacturing rubber-stamping, regardless of anyone's intent.

title: Designing the human step so it's actually done
description: A review requirement that isn't budgeted into anyone's actual workload gets skipped under backlog pressure — designing it to survive that pressure means sampling deliberately, logging overrides, and setting a workload budget that's honest about how long real review takes.

learningObjectives.text: Design a human-review step with a workload budget and sampling rate that survives real backlog pressure
Identify what evidence would show a designed review step is actually being followed in practice, not just on paper

contentSections.body: Halsey's redesigned review screen (from the previous lesson) genuinely requires looking at the comparison data — but three months later, an audit finds override rates dropping again during the last two hours of each Friday, when the week's backlog piles up before the weekend. The screen didn't get worse. The workload did, and nobody had ever set a budget for how many cases a reviewer could actually give real attention to in a shift — so when volume spiked, the unwritten expectation was still "clear the queue," and clearing the queue quietly won.

A review step designed to survive real operating pressure needs a few concrete things a well-designed screen alone doesn't provide:

**A stated workload budget.** If genuine review of a flagged match takes roughly ninety seconds, and a reviewer is scheduled for 300 cases in a shift, the math doesn't work — the budget is either wrong or the review is not actually going to happen at real volume. The budget has to be set from the actual time real review takes, not from whatever throughput the business needs.

**A deliberate sampling rate when full review genuinely isn't feasible**, set on purpose and revisited on a schedule — not left to drift downward under backlog pressure the way Halsey's Friday pattern shows it can. "We review a randomly selected 20% of flagged matches, reassessed quarterly" is a real design decision; "we review whatever we get to" is the same failure mode with a different name.

**Logging that makes the pattern visible before it causes another wrongful denial** — not just an aggregate quarterly audit, but a dashboard a manager actually looks at that would have caught the Friday-afternoon dip within the week it started, not three months later.

contentSections.problem: Design a workload budget and sampling policy for Halsey's screening-analyst review step, given that genuine review takes about 90 seconds per case and the team processes roughly 400 flagged matches a day across four analysts.

steps.label: Establish the honest time cost
steps.work: Genuine review — reading the comparison data, checking for a plausible alternate match — takes about 90 seconds per case, based on timing a sample of careful reviews.
steps.why: The budget has to start from what real review actually costs in time, not from whatever throughput target the business would prefer. Working backward from a desired speed produces a number nobody can actually hit without cutting corners.

steps.label: Check whether full review is feasible at current staffing
steps.work: 400 cases/day ÷ 4 analysts = 100 cases per analyst per day. At 90 seconds each, that's 150 minutes — 2.5 hours of a roughly 7-hour working shift, which is feasible alongside other duties.
steps.why: At this volume and staffing, full review is actually achievable without needing to sample — the earlier Friday-afternoon problem wasn't a capacity problem, it was a scheduling and expectation problem where the same 2.5 hours of review work got compressed into the last two hours before close.

steps.label: Fix the actual cause: workload pacing, not sampling
steps.work: Since full review is feasible on average but collapses under end-of-week compression, the fix is pacing the review workload across the week (a rolling queue with a maximum daily backlog, rather than a Friday-afternoon clearing push) rather than introducing sampling that wasn't otherwise necessary.
steps.why: Sampling is the right tool when full review genuinely isn't feasible at the given volume and staffing. Here it isn't the right tool — the capacity exists, it's just structured to fail under a predictable weekly pattern, which calls for a scheduling fix instead.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure: Halsey is opening a much larger regional contract that will roughly triple flagged-match volume to 1,200 a day, with no plan yet to add screening staff.

blanks.prompt: At 90 seconds per case and the same 4 analysts, how many hours of review work would 1,200 cases/day require per analyst, and is that feasible in a normal shift?
blanks.answer: 1,200 ÷ 4 = 300 cases per analyst; 300 × 90 seconds = 450 minutes, or 7.5 hours — not feasible within a normal shift alongside any other duties
accept: about 7.5 hours per analyst, which doesn't fit in a normal shift
blanks.why: Applying the same honest-cost arithmetic to the new volume shows full review is no longer feasible with current staffing — this is the situation sampling actually exists for, unlike the Friday-afternoon case.

blanks.prompt: Given that full review isn't feasible at the new volume without more staff, what deliberate design decision should replace it — and what should NOT happen instead?
blanks.answer: set a deliberate sampling rate (e.g. review a defined percentage of flagged matches, chosen so the reviewed volume fits the real time budget) and revisit it on a schedule; what should not happen is letting the review rate drift down silently as volume grows past what staff can handle
accept: a stated, deliberate sampling percentage set to fit the actual time budget, reviewed periodically — not an undocumented drift toward reviewing whatever staff get to
blanks.why: This is the core design principle from the lesson text: sampling has to be chosen on purpose to fit a real time budget, and revisited — the failure mode to avoid is the same review rate silently shrinking as volume grows, without anyone deciding that on purpose.

faded.procedure: Start from the honest time cost of a genuine review. Compare that against real volume and staffing to see whether full review is actually feasible. If it is but keeps failing anyway, look for a scheduling or pacing cause rather than reaching for sampling. If it genuinely isn't feasible, set a deliberate sampling rate sized to the real time budget, and put a review date on it rather than letting it drift.

contentSections.body: A review step survives real operating pressure only if its workload budget was set from how long genuine review actually takes, its sampling rate (when full review isn't feasible) was chosen on purpose and revisited on a schedule, and there's logging specific enough to catch a Friday-afternoon-shaped failure within the week it starts, not three months later in a quarterly audit.

title: Practice — Decide Human-in-the-Loop or Not for Eight Steps
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: read a proposed automated step and decide whether it belongs in the money/health/record class, whether the accountability and review design would actually function, or whether it's a genuine automation-bias risk in disguise.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's tests to new automated decisions across several industries
Distinguish a defensible human-in-the-loop design from a rubber stamp with the same nominal structure

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all eight now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Design the Human Checkpoints for a Risky Automation
description: Take one real or realistic automation that touches money, health or record, and design the human checkpoint that actually stays alert: what the reviewer sees, what they decide, and how you'd verify they really looked.

learningObjectives.text: Design a human review checkpoint with a workload budget, visible evidence, and low-friction override for a real automation
Specify concrete evidence that would show whether a designed checkpoint is being followed in practice

contentSections.body: Pick one automation you know — from your own work, a client's, or one described concretely enough to reason about honestly — that touches someone's money, health, or permanent record. Design the human checkpoint for it: not just "a person reviews it," but what they specifically see, what specifically counts as a decision, and what evidence would tell you, a month from now, whether they were actually reviewing or rubber-stamping.

contentSections.title: Your checkpoint design
contentSections.brief: Choose one real automated decision that changes what someone is owed, what care they receive, or what their record says. Design the human checkpoint for it, using this module's tests for the decision class, real accountability, meaningful review, and a workload-realistic design.
contentSections.deliverable: A checkpoint design stating exactly what the reviewer sees, what they decide and how, and what specific evidence would show whether the checkpoint is actually being followed rather than rubber-stamped.

stages.title: Name the decision and confirm it belongs in the class
stages.instructions: Describe the specific automated decision you're designing for. Confirm, in writing, that it belongs in the money/health/record class from this module's first lesson — name the specific, hard-to-reverse consequence to a specific person if it goes wrong.
stages.checkpoint: You have a one-paragraph justification naming the specific consequence, not a general statement that the decision "feels important."

stages.title: Design the accountable role
stages.instructions: Name the specific human role accountable for this decision. Specify what visibility they need into a disputed case (not just a summary) and what authority they need to actually correct a wrong decision, per this module's accountability test.
stages.checkpoint: The role has both a visibility requirement and an authority requirement stated explicitly, not just a name.

stages.title: Design the review screen and workload budget
stages.instructions: Specify what the reviewer sees by default, what action constitutes approval versus override, and the relative friction of each. Then estimate a realistic time cost per genuine review and check it against realistic volume and staffing — decide full review or a deliberately sized sampling rate, and say why.
stages.checkpoint: The design addresses default visibility, explicit approval action, override friction, and a workload budget grounded in a real time estimate — not just "a human reviews it."

stages.title: Specify the evidence that would catch a collapse
stages.instructions: Name the specific, measurable signals — like the ones from this module's automation-bias lesson — that would show this checkpoint had degraded into a rubber stamp, and how often you'd check them.
stages.checkpoint: At least two concrete, measurable signals are named (e.g. time-per-case, override rate against case complexity), with a stated check frequency.

rubric.criterion: The decision is justified as belonging in the money/health/record class
rubric.meets: A specific, hard-to-reverse consequence to a specific person is named, not a general importance claim.

rubric.criterion: The accountable role has real visibility and authority, not just a name
rubric.meets: The design states specifically what the role can see and what it has the power to change.

rubric.criterion: The review screen design avoids the rubber-stamp failure modes
rubric.meets: Evidence is visible by default, approval requires a genuine action, and override is no harder than approval.

rubric.criterion: The workload budget is grounded in a real time estimate against real volume
rubric.meets: A specific per-case time estimate is checked against staffing and volume, with a stated full-review-or-sampling decision and reasoning.

rubric.criterion: The design names concrete, measurable signals of collapse into rubber-stamping
rubric.meets: At least two specific, checkable metrics are named, with a stated review cadence.

rubric.criterion: A colleague could implement the checkpoint without asking a follow-up question
rubric.meets: Every element — visibility, authority, screen design, workload, monitoring — is specific enough to build from.

contentSections.body: "A human reviews it" is not a checkpoint design. What the reviewer sees, what counts as a decision, how much a genuine review actually costs in time, and what would reveal the review has quietly stopped happening — that's the deliverable, and it's what separates real oversight from a rubber stamp with an extra click.

title: Checkpoint — The Judgement You Can't Remove
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous one, and two pulling further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's accountability and review-design distinctions, and connect them to earlier mechanism-selection and capability material

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — The Judgement You Can't Remove

questions.from: This module — The Judgement You Can't Remove

options.label: Whether the step runs at high volume
Whether a wrong decision changes what a specific person is owed, what care they receive, or what their record says, in a way that's hard to reverse
Whether the step is central to the company's revenue

questions.explanation: Halsey's criminal-record match qualified because a wrong match attached a disqualifying record to the wrong person in a way that's hard to undo — volume and revenue centrality were both shown to be the wrong signals to trust.

questions.from: This module — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: What does a named accountable role actually need in order to provide real accountability, not just exist on an org chart?

options.label: A clear job title
Visibility into the specific disputed case, plus real authority to correct the decision
A fast response time to complaints

questions.explanation: Halsey's QA team had a title but neither database access to re-examine the match nor documented authority to overturn it — a role without both is decorative, not functional accountability.

questions.from: This module — The Judgement You Can't Remove

options.label: There's no flaw — a matching rate is strong evidence review is working
That exact pattern is equally consistent with automation bias having fully set in — reviewers rubber-stamping the algorithm would produce the same number as reviewers genuinely re-verifying it
The accuracy figure itself must be wrong

questions.explanation: Halsey's audit memo made exactly this mistake — the metric can't distinguish real verification from rubber-stamping, so it shouldn't be cited as reassurance on its own.

questions.from: This module — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: What design feature most directly separates a meaningful review screen from a rubber stamp with an extra click?

options.label: Whether the screen has a modern visual design
Whether comparison evidence is visible by default and disagreeing with the algorithm costs no more effort than agreeing with it
Whether the screen loads quickly

questions.explanation: Halsey's original screen hid the comparison data behind an optional link and pre-selected "Approve" — the redesign fixed exactly these two things, which is what separates real review from a click that happens to be labeled "review."

questions.from: This module — The Judgement You Can't Remove

options.label: Whatever throughput the business needs to hit
An honest estimate of how long genuine review actually takes, checked against real volume and staffing
The fastest time any single reviewer has ever completed a case in

The complete mapping from input to one correct output is already written down somewhere, and two competent people would always agree

The correct answer depends on facts the input doesn't reliably carry, over a set of possible inputs no table could enumerate

title: Where the data lives, and what shape it's in
description: Before designing anything, map where the data a proposed automation would actually run on lives — which systems, which formats, and how much of it is a spreadsheet or a paper note that doesn't show up on any architecture diagram.

learningObjectives.text: Map the real, complete set of systems a proposed automation's input data actually comes from
Recognize shadow data sources (spreadsheets, paper, personal notes) that a system-of-record diagram would miss

contentSections.body: Solstice Home Health, a home-care agency coordinating nurse visits for homebound patients, asks a consultant to "just plug in an AI" that routes incoming referrals to the right care team based on urgency and specialty needed. The consultant asks where referral data lives. The answer, after two follow-up meetings: some referrals arrive through the agency's scheduling software, some by fax that an intake coordinator retypes into that same software, some as a phone call the coordinator summarizes from memory an hour later, and a meaningful fraction as a sticky note on a specific coordinator's monitor for the referrals she "just knows how to route" from twenty years of experience. None of this showed up on the systems diagram Solstice's office manager drew in the first meeting.

Mapping the data landscape before designing any automation means finding the actual sources an input would come from, not the systems-of-record a client's diagram claims are authoritative. A useful distinction: **systems of record** are where a client believes the data officially lives — usually a database or a named piece of software. **Shadow sources** are where a meaningful fraction of the real data actually lives — spreadsheets, sticky notes, someone's memory, a workaround built to handle a case the official system doesn't support well.

Shadow sources aren't a sign of a badly run business — they're what happens whenever a rule handles the common case and staff quietly built something to handle everything the rule doesn't. The problem for automation specifically is that a system built to read only the system of record will silently miss the fraction of real cases that live in the shadow sources, and nobody may notice until those specific cases start failing — which, without deliberate investigation, could take months, because the automation looks like it's working fine on everything it can actually see.

contentSections.scenario: Solstice's referrals arrive through four channels the intake coordinator described once asked directly: (1) the scheduling software's referral intake form, filled out by the referring hospital's discharge planner; (2) a fax that gets manually retyped into the same software; (3) a phone call the coordinator summarizes from memory into a sticky note, later transcribed when there's time; (4) a coordinator's personal knowledge of which patients "always go to the Tuesday team" based on history that exists only in her head.
contentSections.question: Which of these four sources would a proposed AI referral-router, built to read only the scheduling software's database, completely fail to see?

options.label: Channels 2, 3 and 4 — the fax, the phone summary before transcription, and the coordinator's personal knowledge
Only channel 1 — the direct intake form
None — all four eventually end up in the scheduling software

feedback.channels-2-3-4: Right. Channel 2's fax exists only on paper until retyped — a router reading the database sees nothing until that retyping happens, which introduces a lag and a transcription-error risk the router can't detect. Channel 3's phone summary is a sticky note until "there's time" to transcribe it — an unpredictable delay a router has no visibility into. Channel 4 never becomes structured data at all; it's a coordinator's judgment the automation would need to somehow capture or it simply loses that routing logic entirely.
feedback.channel-1-only: This has it backwards — channel 1 is precisely the one source a router reading the scheduling database would see cleanly and immediately, since it's entered directly by the referring hospital's staff with no intermediate step.
feedback.none: Technically, channels 2 and 3 do eventually end up in the software — but "eventually" is doing a lot of work here. A router reading the database in real time would miss them for however long the retyping or transcription delay lasts, and channel 4 never becomes structured data at all, so it never reaches the database regardless of how long you wait.

contentSections.concept: The systems-of-record diagram tells you where a client believes the data lives. The actual data landscape includes every shadow source that feeds into or around those systems — and an automation designed only against the official diagram will quietly miss exactly the fraction of real cases the shadow sources exist to handle, with a failure that looks like nothing, not an error, until someone goes looking.

contentSections.scenario: You're interviewing Solstice staff to build a complete data landscape map before proposing anything. Some of what you hear is a real shadow source worth mapping; some is a normal, already-captured part of the official system.
contentSections.question: Select every signal that you've found a genuine shadow data source that a systems diagram would miss.

items.label: Staff describe a workaround they built themselves to handle a case type the official system doesn't support well
A specific piece of routing logic exists only in one staff member's memory or personal notes, never entered into any system
Information arrives correctly but sits ungentered in a non-digital form for an unpredictable period before someone transcribes it
A field on the standard intake form that every referral fills in the same way
The scheduling software was recently upgraded to a newer version
Staff say they generally prefer phone calls to email for referrals

explanation.workaround-exists: Applicable. A self-built workaround is the clearest signature of a shadow source — it exists precisely because the official system doesn't handle something, and it's exactly the fraction an automation built against only the official system would miss.
explanation.lives-in-head: Applicable, and the hardest kind to map, because it isn't even written down informally — it's tacit knowledge that would need a deliberate interview to surface, let alone digitize.
explanation.delay-before-entry: Applicable. Even correctly-captured information is effectively invisible to a system reading the database in real time for however long it sits untranscribed — this delay is itself a shape of shadow data worth documenting even when the ultimate destination is the official system.
explanation.standard-form-field: Not applicable — this is exactly the opposite signal. A field filled in the same way on a standard form is precisely the closed, already-captured case a systems diagram correctly represents.
explanation.recent-software-update: Not applicable as evidence of a shadow source. A software upgrade is a real fact worth knowing for other reasons, but it doesn't by itself indicate any data lives outside the official system.
explanation.staff-prefer-phone: Not applicable on its own — a channel preference only becomes a shadow-source signal if you learn what specifically happens to the information after the phone call, which channel 3 above makes concrete. A stated preference alone isn't yet evidence of a gap.

contentSections.synthesis: The three signals that hold up all point at the same underlying fact: some information exists, and is real, and is not where the official system would lead you to look for it, or not yet in a form the system can see. The three that don't are either evidence the official system is working as intended, or facts that need one more concrete detail before they tell you anything about where data actually lives.

contentSections.body: Before designing an automation, map where the input data actually lives — not just the systems of record a client's diagram names, but the shadow sources (workarounds, tacit knowledge, information sitting untranscribed) that a diagram alone will never reveal, and that an automation built against the diagram alone will silently fail to see.

title: Volume, labelling and the examples you'd need
description: A classifier is only as good as the labelled examples behind it — and "we've been doing this for years" doesn't mean the labels exist anywhere a model, or a person building one, could actually use them.

learningObjectives.text: Determine whether a proposed classification task has the volume and labelled ground truth it would actually need
Identify viable options when historical labels don't already exist

contentSections.title: Years of experience, zero labelled examples

contentSections.body: Solstice wants a classifier that reads a new referral and tags its urgency — same-day, this-week, routine — so the router in the previous lesson knows how fast to act. The office manager is confident: "We've been triaging referrals like this for eight years, we have thousands of them in the system." What Solstice actually has is thousands of referrals with an outcome (which team eventually saw the patient, and when) but no field anywhere recording what urgency level was assigned at intake, by whom, or why. Eight years of experience produced eight years of decisions. It didn't produce eight years of labels.

A classification task needs two things that "we've done this for years" doesn't automatically supply: enough volume of past cases, and those cases labelled with the specific category the model needs to predict — recorded at the time, in a retrievable field, ideally by more than one person so you can check whether people agree.

What Solstice has is closer to an outcome record than a label: it knows when a patient was eventually seen, but not what urgency call was actually made at intake, which is a different fact. This is the cold-start problem — a business can be genuinely expert at a judgment and still have nothing usable to train or evaluate a model against, because expertise lived in people's heads and time-pressured phone calls, not in a labelled field anyone thought to capture.

contentSections.scenario: Solstice's office manager proposes: "Let's just use how quickly each referral was actually seen as the urgency label — if a patient was seen same-day, label that referral 'same-day urgency.'"
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in using "time to being seen" as a stand-in for the urgency label the classifier actually needs to predict?

options.label: Time-to-seen reflects everything that happened after intake — team availability, scheduling conflicts, a coordinator's workload that day — not just the urgency judgment made at the moment of intake, so it's a noisy, contaminated stand-in for the actual label needed
There isn't enough referral volume to use this approach at all
The scheduling software stores dates in a format the model can't read

feedback.outcome-not-decision: Right. A patient seen same-day might have been genuinely urgent — or might have been routine, but happened to land on a day with an open slot, while a genuinely urgent case from a busy week waited two days because every team was full. Using the outcome as a proxy for the decision bakes staffing noise into the label, and a model trained on it would learn to predict scheduling luck as much as actual urgency.
feedback.not-enough-data: Volume isn't the stated problem here — Solstice has thousands of referrals. The problem is that none of them carry the specific label the task needs, which more volume of the same unlabeled data doesn't fix.
feedback.wrong-format: This is a solvable, mechanical data-formatting issue, not the actual flaw in this specific proposal — even with a perfectly formatted date field, time-to-seen still isn't the same fact as the urgency judgment made at intake.

contentSections.mechanism: A usable label has to reflect the specific judgment the model needs to reproduce, recorded at the time it was made — not a downstream outcome shaped by other factors that happened afterward. Confusing the two produces a model that learns to predict the noise (staffing, scheduling luck) instead of the signal (the actual urgency call), and it can look like it's working in testing while being wrong for reasons nobody can see in the aggregate accuracy number.

contentSections.title: What to do when the labels genuinely don't exist

contentSections.body: When historical labels don't exist, there are a few real options, and "give up on the project" isn't usually the first one worth reaching for. **Retrospective labelling**: have current clinical staff review a sample of past referrals and assign the urgency label now, based on what they know today — slower and imperfect (memory fades, hindsight creeps in) but produces a real, usable dataset. **A forward-looking capture period**: start recording the label at the moment of intake going forward, accept that the model can't be built yet, and revisit once enough labelled volume accumulates — often weeks to months, not years, for a business with real referral volume. **Rules bootstrap**: build a simple, explicit rule set from staff's stated criteria (certain diagnosis codes always route same-day, for instance) as a first version, which also has the side benefit of surfacing disagreements between staff about what the criteria even are before any model gets built on top of them.

contentSections.scenario: You're advising Solstice on which labelling approach fits their situation: thousands of unlabeled historical referrals, real ongoing referral volume of about 40/week, and clinical staff who are available for a few hours a month but not for a large one-time project.
contentSections.question: Select every consideration that should genuinely shape the recommendation.

items.label: How much staff time is realistically available for a labelling effort, given other duties
Whether the client needs a working classifier immediately or can accept a rules-based first version while labels accumulate
How reliable retrospective labels would be, given how much time has passed since the original referrals and how well staff would actually remember the reasoning
Which scheduling software vendor Solstice currently uses
How many care teams Solstice currently has
Whether Solstice's office is in a rural or urban area

explanation.staff-time-budget: Applicable. A retrospective-labelling plan that assumes more staff hours than are actually available isn't a real plan — this directly decides whether that approach is even feasible here.
explanation.how-fast-model-needed: Applicable. If Solstice needs something working now, a rules bootstrap while labels accumulate is the realistic path; if there's no urgency, a forward-capture period alone might be enough.
explanation.memory-decay: Applicable. Retrospective labels on referrals from three years ago, recalled by staff who may not remember the specifics, are far less trustworthy than labels on referrals from last month — this should directly affect which historical window, if any, gets used.
explanation.software-brand: Not applicable to the labelling-approach decision — which vendor Solstice uses doesn't change how much labelled ground truth exists or how it should be gathered.
explanation.team-size: Not applicable here. The number of care teams affects routing logic downstream, but it doesn't change whether or how urgency labels should be gathered.
explanation.office-location: Not applicable. Geography has no bearing on this specific data-readiness question.

contentSections.synthesis: The three considerations that matter are all about whether a labelling approach is actually achievable and trustworthy given Solstice's real constraints — staff time, urgency, and how much to trust human memory of past decisions. The three that don't are real facts about Solstice that matter elsewhere in the engagement, but they don't move this specific decision about how to get usable labels.

contentSections.body: "We've done this for years" tells you a business has expertise. It doesn't tell you the expertise was ever captured as a labelled example anywhere retrievable — and a downstream outcome (when a patient was eventually seen) is not the same fact as the judgment made at the moment of intake. When labels genuinely don't exist, retrospective labelling, a forward capture period, and a rules bootstrap are three real starting points, not a reason to give up.

title: Personal data: what may leave the building
description: Sending patient data to a third-party AI vendor's API isn't a technical detail to sort out later — it's a decision with legal exposure, existing patient promises, and vendor-retention terms that have to be checked before, not after, the first real record is sent.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what must be checked before sending personal data to a third-party AI vendor
Distinguish a vendor's marketing privacy claims from the specific contractual terms that actually govern data handling

contentSections.title: "We'll just send it to the API"

contentSections.body: The urgency-classification model for Solstice's referrals, once built, needs to run on real patient intake text — symptom descriptions, diagnosis notes, sometimes a family member's account of what happened. A junior engineer on the project suggests the fastest path: send the referral text straight to a general-purpose AI vendor's API and get a classification back. This works technically within an afternoon. It's also a decision, made in an afternoon, about whether protected patient health information may leave Solstice's systems and be processed by a third party — a decision that, done wrong, can violate both healthcare privacy law and promises Solstice has already made its own patients in writing.

Before any personal data leaves a client's own systems for a third-party AI vendor, a few specific things need checking, not assumed: **Is there a signed data processing agreement (a Business Associate Agreement, in U.S. healthcare specifically) with the vendor** — sending health data to a vendor without one is often a compliance violation regardless of how the vendor's product performs. **What does the vendor actually do with the data after the API call** — some vendors' default terms allow using submitted data to improve their own models, which is a very different promise than "we process it and discard it," and the difference is usually in a specific contract clause, not the marketing page. **Where is the vendor's infrastructure located**, if the client operates under a data-residency requirement. **What did the client already promise its own patients** — a privacy notice patients signed may already specify who their data can be shared with, and a new AI vendor may not be covered by that existing consent at all.

The fix isn't always "never send data to a vendor" — sometimes it's a properly executed agreement, sometimes it's de-identifying the data first (stripping names, exact dates, and other identifiers before it ever leaves), and sometimes it's choosing a vendor offering on-premises or private deployment specifically because the data can't leave at all. Which fix applies depends on checking the specific facts, not defaulting to whichever is fastest to implement.

contentSections.scenario: You're auditing the proposed Solstice-to-vendor data flow before anything goes live. Some of what you find genuinely matters to whether this is compliant and safe; some is a real consideration for a different decision entirely.
contentSections.question: Select every finding that should block or reshape the data flow as currently proposed.

items.label: No Business Associate Agreement has been signed with the vendor, and the data includes protected health information
The vendor's default terms allow using submitted data to improve their own models unless the client opts out in writing
Solstice's existing patient privacy notice doesn't mention sharing data with third-party AI vendors at all
The vendor's per-call price is higher than a competitor's
The vendor's published uptime guarantee is 99.5%
The vendor was founded two years ago

explanation.no-baa: Applicable, and likely disqualifying as-is. Sending protected health information to a vendor with no signed agreement covering how they may handle it is a real compliance exposure regardless of the vendor's technical quality.
explanation.training-use: Applicable. A default that allows the vendor to use submitted patient data to improve its own models is a materially different promise from "process and discard," and needs to be explicitly opted out of — or the vendor needs to be ruled out — before any real patient data goes through it.
explanation.notice-silent: Applicable. If patients were never told their data might be shared with a third-party AI vendor, sending it there may violate the specific promise Solstice already made them in writing, independent of whether the vendor itself is trustworthy.
explanation.vendor-price: Not applicable to whether the data flow is compliant or safe — pricing is a real factor in vendor selection, but it doesn't touch any of the three findings above.
explanation.vendor-uptime: Not applicable here. Uptime is a real operational concern for reliability, but it says nothing about what happens to the data once it's sent.
explanation.vendor-founded-recently: Not applicable on its own. A newer vendor isn't automatically less trustworthy — what matters is the specific contract terms and compliance posture, not company age.

contentSections.synthesis: The three findings that matter are all specific facts about what actually happens to the data and what Solstice already promised about it — an agreement, a data-use default, and a patient notice. The three that don't are all real vendor-selection factors, just not ones that touch whether this specific data flow is compliant or consistent with what patients were told.

contentSections.body: Whether personal data may leave the building is a specific question with specific, checkable answers — a signed data agreement, the vendor's actual data-use terms, and what the client already promised its own users — not a technical detail to sort out after the pipeline is already sending real records.

title: Data that's wrong in a consistent, invisible way
description: Some data-entry defaults and workarounds corrupt a field so consistently that the error doesn't show up as noise — it shows up as a confident, uniform pattern that looks like signal, and a model trained on it faithfully reproduces the mistake.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a systematically-wrong field is masquerading as clean, consistent data
