Trace a consistent data error back to its likely operational cause (a default value, a time-pressured shortcut)

contentSections.title: The urgency field that was always "routine"

contentSections.body: Once Solstice starts forward-capturing urgency labels at intake (the previous lesson's fix), a data engineer building the training set notices something odd: 78% of referrals are labelled "routine." That's not itself suspicious — most referrals probably are routine. What's suspicious is which specific coordinator's referrals are 78% routine: it's the same figure for every coordinator, on every shift, regardless of referral source or patient complexity. It turns out the intake form's urgency field defaults to "routine" when opened, and under time pressure, coordinators frequently submit the form without changing it — meaning a meaningful fraction of the "routine" label isn't a urgency judgment at all. It's a default nobody got around to overriding.

This is a distinct failure from both of the earlier lessons in this module: it isn't a shadow source the system can't see (the data is right there in the field), and it isn't a missing label (there's a label in every row). It's a field that's systematically wrong in a way that looks exactly like clean, consistent data — because the corruption itself is consistent. A field that's randomly wrong 20% of the time announces itself as noisy; a field that's wrong in the same specific way every time a specific condition holds (time pressure, a specific coordinator, a specific referral source) looks like signal, and a model trained on it learns the default-value artifact as if it were a real pattern in urgency.

The tell to look for: a suspiciously uniform rate across a dimension that should show real variation (different coordinators, different shifts, different referral sources should not, in reality, all produce identical proportions of any given category), combined with the value matching a form default, a first option in a dropdown, or some other structural feature of how the data gets entered rather than a fact about the patient.

contentSections.code: Solstice's data engineer's initial write-up: "Urgency label distribution looks clean and consistent — 78% routine, 15% this-week, 7% same-day, holding steady across every coordinator and shift. Good sign that the labelling process is reliable and we're ready to train."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in reading this consistency as a good sign?

options.label: A rate this uniform across every coordinator and shift is itself suspicious, not reassuring — real urgency judgments, made by different people about different patients on different days, should show some natural variation, and a rate that never moves looks more like a shared structural artifact (a form default) than a shared clinical judgment
The sample size isn't large enough to draw any conclusion yet
78/15/7 doesn't add up to 100, so the numbers themselves are wrong

feedback.uniform-suspicious: Right. Consistency that's too perfect, across a dimension that should show real variation if it reflected genuine judgment, is exactly the signature this lesson describes. The data engineer read "looks clean" as "is correct," when the specific kind of clean here — identical across every coordinator and shift — is the tell that something structural, not clinical, is producing the number.
feedback.sample-too-small: Sample size isn't the issue the write-up should be flagging — the issue is that the pattern itself, however large the sample, is more consistent with a data-entry artifact than with genuine variation in patient urgency across many different people and days.
feedback.wrong-percentages: 78 + 15 + 7 = 100, so the arithmetic is fine — this distracts from the actual, substantive flaw in how the consistency is being interpreted.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The instinct to treat a clean, consistent distribution as a good sign is usually right for genuinely independent measurements — but urgency judgments made by different coordinators, about different patients, are supposed to vary with the actual clinical picture. A rate that holds identically across every coordinator and shift is the opposite of what real, independent clinical judgment would produce, and is far more consistent with everyone hitting the same default under the same time pressure. The fix here isn't more data — it's investigating the form itself, which the next step of this lesson makes concrete.

contentSections.body: A field that's wrong in a consistent, structural way — a form default nobody overrides, a dropdown's first option, a shortcut everyone takes under the same pressure — doesn't look noisy. It looks clean, uniform, and reassuring, which is exactly what makes it dangerous: a model trained on it learns the artifact as if it were the real pattern. Suspiciously perfect consistency across a dimension that should show real variation is the tell.

title: Retention, deletion, and what a client has promised its users
description: A proposed pipeline can be technically sound and still violate a promise the client already made its own users in writing — checking a data-retention and deletion promise against what a vendor pipeline would actually do is part of the data-readiness assessment, not a legal afterthought.

learningObjectives.text: Check a proposed AI pipeline's data handling against a client's existing, written promises to its users about retention and deletion
Identify where a vendor's data-retention practice conflicts with a client's stated policy, even when the vendor's practice is standard for the industry

contentSections.title: The promise nobody checked against the pipeline

contentSections.body: Solstice's own patient privacy notice — the document every new patient signs — states that Solstice deletes identifiable records two years after a patient's care ends, "except as required by law." The consultant, finalizing the urgency-classification pipeline, asks a simple question nobody on the project had asked yet: does the AI vendor's data-retention policy also delete Solstice's submitted patient records after two years, or does it keep them indefinitely, or for its own separate retention period, once they've been sent through the API? Nobody knew. The pipeline had been designed entirely around whether it worked technically — accuracy, latency, cost — and never checked against a promise Solstice had already made in writing to the people whose data it was.

This is a distinct check from the earlier lesson on what may leave the building at all — that question is about whether sending the data anywhere is permitted; this one is about whether a pipeline that's otherwise permitted still honors what the client specifically committed to. It's a real, common gap, because a client's privacy notice is usually written by a different part of the organization than the one commissioning an AI pipeline, and neither side automatically checks the other's commitments against the new project's actual data flow.

The concrete check: read the client's existing privacy notice or data policy for any stated retention period, deletion commitment, or specific list of parties data may be shared with. Then check the proposed vendor's actual retention practice — not their marketing claim, their contract terms — against that promise specifically. A vendor's standard retention period being reasonable, or common in the industry, doesn't matter if it's longer than what the client specifically promised its own users; the client's promise is the bar, not general industry practice.

contentSections.problem: Check whether the proposed AI vendor's pipeline for Solstice's referral data honors Solstice's existing two-year deletion promise.

steps.label: Read the client's actual written promise
steps.work: Solstice's patient privacy notice states identifiable records are deleted two years after care ends, except as required by law.
steps.why: This is the specific commitment the pipeline needs to be checked against — not a general industry norm, not what would be reasonable, but the exact promise Solstice already made in writing.

steps.label: Read the vendor's actual retention terms, not their marketing page
steps.work: The vendor's contract (not their public marketing copy) states submitted data is retained for 90 days for abuse-monitoring purposes, then deleted, unless the client has opted into the vendor's model-improvement program, which retains data indefinitely.
steps.why: Marketing pages often state general principles ("we take privacy seriously") without the operative retention period, which only appears in the actual contract — the operative terms are what has to be checked, not the framing.

steps.label: Compare and identify the actual conflict
steps.work: 90-day abuse-monitoring retention is well within Solstice's two-year promise and poses no conflict. The optional model-improvement program, if enabled, would retain data indefinitely — directly conflicting with the two-year deletion promise the moment it's turned on.
steps.why: The two vendor terms aren't equally risky — one is compatible with the existing promise, and the other is a straightforward violation of it if ever enabled, even inadvertently by a default setting.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure: Solstice's privacy notice separately states patient data "will not be shared with third parties for marketing purposes." The AI vendor's contract states that anonymized, aggregated usage statistics (not individual patient records) may be used in the vendor's own promotional case studies.

blanks.prompt: What's the client's actual written promise here, stated precisely?
blanks.answer: patient data will not be shared with third parties for marketing purposes
accept: no sharing of patient data with third parties for marketing
blanks.why: Getting the exact wording of the promise matters, because whether the vendor's practice conflicts with it depends on precisely what was promised — a promise about identifiable patient data reads differently against an anonymized, aggregated use than it would against a promise with no such qualifier.

blanks.prompt: Does the vendor's practice (anonymized, aggregated usage statistics in promotional case studies) actually conflict with this specific promise — and what follow-up question, if any, would you still need to ask before concluding either way?
blanks.answer: it's a genuine gray area rather than a clean match or conflict — the promise is about 'patient data,' and whether truly anonymized, aggregated statistics still count as 'patient data' under this promise (and under applicable law) needs a specific follow-up question, not an assumption either way; also worth checking exactly how the anonymization is done and whether it could be reversed
accept: ambiguous — needs to confirm whether anonymized aggregate statistics count as covered patient data, and how robust the anonymization actually is
blanks.why: Not every check in this lesson resolves to a clean yes-or-no — this is deliberately a case where the honest answer is a specific follow-up question, because 'anonymized' and 'aggregated' are doing real work in the vendor's claim and need to be verified, not taken at face value, before concluding whether the client's promise is actually being honored.

faded.procedure: Read the client's exact written promise, not a paraphrase of it. Read the vendor's actual contract terms, not their marketing framing. Compare the two specifically — and where the comparison isn't clean, name the precise follow-up question needed rather than guessing at an answer either way.

contentSections.body: A pipeline that's technically sound and legally permitted can still violate a promise the client already made its own users in writing. Checking the client's actual privacy notice against the vendor's actual contract terms — not marketing claims on either side — is part of a data-readiness assessment, and where the comparison isn't clean, the honest answer is naming the specific follow-up question, not guessing.

title: Practice — Assess Data Readiness for Seven Proposed Automations
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: read a proposed automation and its actual data situation, and apply this module's tests — shadow sources, real labels vs outcomes, what may leave the building, consistent-but-wrong fields, and retention promises.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's data-readiness tests to new automations across several industries
Distinguish a genuinely data-ready proposal from one with a specific, nameable gap

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run a Data-Readiness Assessment on a Real Dataset
description: Take a real or realistic proposed automation and its actual data, and produce a go / go-with-conditions / no verdict with the evidence for it, covering data landscape, labels, what may leave the building, hidden corruption, and retention promises.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a data-readiness verdict for a real proposed automation, with evidence for each of this module's five checks
Distinguish a go, a go-with-conditions, and a no verdict based on the severity and fixability of what's found

contentSections.body: Pick one real or realistically-detailed proposed automation you can investigate honestly — from your own work, a client's, or one you can research concretely enough to reason about. Run the full data-readiness assessment this module builds toward: where the data actually lives, whether real labels exist, what may leave the building, whether anything is wrong in a consistent way, and whether the pipeline honors any existing promises to the people the data is about.

contentSections.title: Your data-readiness assessment
contentSections.brief: Choose one real proposed automation and investigate its actual data situation, not the idealized version a systems diagram or a pitch deck would describe. Produce a verdict — go, go-with-conditions, or no — with the specific evidence behind it.
contentSections.deliverable: A data-readiness assessment covering data landscape, label availability, personal-data handling, data-quality risk, and retention/promise alignment, ending in a go / go-with-conditions / no verdict with evidence stated per finding.

stages.title: Map the real data landscape
stages.instructions: Identify every system of record and every shadow source (workarounds, tacit knowledge, information that sits untranscribed) the proposed automation's input would actually need to see. Interview or research specifically for shadow sources — they rarely appear on the first pass.
stages.checkpoint: You have a landscape map naming at least one shadow source in addition to the official systems of record, or a documented finding that none exists (with your evidence for that conclusion).

stages.title: Check label availability and personal-data handling
stages.instructions: If the automation involves classification or prediction, determine whether real, correctly-timed labels exist (not a downstream outcome standing in for the actual judgment) and what volume is available. Separately, if personal data is involved, check what's actually permitted to leave the client's systems — agreements, vendor data-use terms, existing consent.
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific finding on label availability (exists / partially exists / doesn't exist, with why) and a specific finding on what's permitted to leave the building, not a general impression of either.

stages.title: Check for consistent-but-wrong data and retention alignment
stages.instructions: Look for any field that's suspiciously uniform across a dimension that should show real variation, and investigate its likely structural cause. Separately, check the client's actual written promises about data retention or sharing against the proposed pipeline's actual practice.
stages.checkpoint: You have a specific finding (or a documented absence of one) for consistent-but-wrong data, and a specific comparison of the client's stated promise against the pipeline's actual practice.

stages.title: Write the verdict with evidence
stages.instructions: Assemble your findings into a go / go-with-conditions / no verdict. If go-with-conditions, state the specific conditions (what has to be fixed or checked before this proceeds). Every claim in the verdict should trace to a specific finding from stages 1-3.
stages.checkpoint: The verdict is stated clearly, and every supporting claim traces to a specific, named finding rather than a general impression.

rubric.criterion: The data landscape includes shadow sources, not just official systems of record
rubric.meets: At least one genuine shadow source is named, or a documented, evidenced conclusion that none exists.

rubric.criterion: The label finding distinguishes real labels from a downstream outcome standing in for them
rubric.meets: The assessment explicitly checks whether available data reflects the actual judgment needed, not a correlated but different fact.

rubric.criterion: The personal-data finding is specific, not general reassurance
rubric.meets: A specific agreement, vendor term, or consent gap is named, not just "we should check with legal."

rubric.criterion: The consistent-but-wrong-data check looks for suspicious uniformity, not just obvious errors
rubric.meets: The assessment explicitly considers whether any clean-looking field could be a structural artifact rather than genuine signal.

rubric.criterion: The retention/promise check compares the client's actual written commitment to the vendor's actual practice
rubric.meets: Both sides of the comparison are specific and sourced, not paraphrased from memory.

rubric.criterion: The verdict and any conditions are traceable to specific findings
rubric.meets: A reader could reconstruct why the verdict was reached from the findings alone, without asking a follow-up question.

contentSections.body: A data-readiness assessment that stops at "do we have data" hasn't actually assessed anything. The verdict comes from five specific checks — where it really lives, whether real labels exist, what may leave the building, whether anything is wrong in a consistent way, and whether the pipeline honors what was already promised — each with its own evidence.

title: Checkpoint — The Data You Actually Have
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous one, and two pulling further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's data-readiness distinctions, and connect them to earlier accountability and mechanism-selection material

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — The Data You Actually Have

questions.from: This module — The Data You Actually Have
questions.prompt: What is a "shadow data source," and why does it matter for a proposed automation?

options.label: A backup copy of the official database

A real source of input data — a workaround, tacit knowledge, an untranscribed note — that a systems-of-record diagram wouldn't show, and that an automation built only against the official system would silently miss
A system that's been deprecated but is still technically running

questions.explanation: Solstice's fax, phone summaries, and one coordinator's personal routing knowledge were all real shadow sources a router built against the scheduling database alone would completely fail to see.

questions.from: This module — The Data You Actually Have
questions.prompt: Solstice has thousands of historical referrals with a recorded outcome (when the patient was eventually seen) but no recorded urgency judgment at intake. Why can't "time to being seen" substitute for a real urgency label?

options.label: It can substitute fine — being seen quickly means the case was urgent
Time-to-seen reflects downstream factors like staffing and scheduling luck, not just the urgency judgment made at intake, so it's a noisy, contaminated stand-in for the actual label needed
The dates are stored in an unreadable format

questions.explanation: A model trained on time-to-seen as a proxy label would learn to predict scheduling luck as much as actual urgency — the outcome and the decision are two different facts.

questions.from: This module — The Data You Actually Have
questions.prompt: Before sending patient data to a third-party AI vendor, what's the first thing that needs checking?

options.label: Whether the vendor's product is technically accurate
Whether a data processing agreement is in place and what the vendor's actual data-use terms are, not their marketing claims
How much the vendor charges per API call

questions.explanation: The compliance and consent questions — a signed agreement, real retention terms, and what patients were already told — have to be resolved before any real data flows, independent of the vendor's technical quality.

questions.from: This module — The Data You Actually Have
questions.prompt: A data field looks clean and consistent — the same distribution across every coordinator and shift. Why might this be a warning sign rather than reassurance?

options.label: It isn't a warning sign — consistency is always a good sign in a dataset

Real, independent human judgments made by different people on different days should show some natural variation — a rate that's identical everywhere is more consistent with a shared structural artifact, like a form default, than genuine clinical judgment
It suggests the sample size is too small

questions.explanation: Solstice's 78% "routine" figure holding identically across every coordinator and shift traced back to a form default nobody was overriding under time pressure — not a real clinical pattern.

questions.from: This module — The Data You Actually Have
questions.prompt: A vendor's data retention practice is reasonable and standard for its industry, but longer than what the client explicitly promised its own users in writing. What's the correct standard to check against?

options.label: General industry practice — if it's standard, it's fine
The client's own specific written promise to its users, which is the bar regardless of what's standard elsewhere
Whichever is longer, since more retention is generally safer

questions.explanation: Solstice's two-year deletion promise is the specific commitment the pipeline has to honor — a vendor's own reasonable, industry-standard retention period is beside the point if it exceeds what was actually promised.

questions.from: Previous module — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: What actually determines whether a decision belongs in the class that needs a named human owner, regardless of average accuracy?

options.label: Whether the step runs at high volume
Whether a wrong decision changes what a specific person is owed, what care they receive, or what their record says, in a way that's hard to reverse
Whether the step is central to the company's revenue

questions.explanation: This is the same class Solstice's urgency triage sits in — a wrong routing decision changes what care a specific patient receives, which is exactly why this module's data-readiness checks matter so much for it specifically.

questions.from: Previous module — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: An override rate that closely tracks an algorithm's own accuracy rate is being cited as proof a human review step is working. What's the flaw?

options.label: There's no flaw — a matching rate is strong evidence review is working
That exact pattern is equally consistent with automation bias having fully set in — reviewers rubber-stamping the algorithm would produce the same number as reviewers genuinely re-verifying it
The accuracy figure itself must be wrong

questions.explanation: This is the same shape of trap as the checkpoint's earlier question about suspiciously uniform data — a number that looks reassuring can be equally consistent with the thing you're worried about having already happened.

questions.from: Previous module — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: What does a named accountable role actually need in order to provide real accountability, not just exist on an org chart?

options.label: A clear job title
Visibility into the specific disputed case, plus real authority to correct the decision
A fast response time to complaints

questions.explanation: A named role without genuine visibility or authority is decorative — the same lesson applies whether the underlying issue is a wrongful denial or a data-handling promise nobody actually checked.

questions.from: Two modules back — What These Systems Can Actually Do
questions.prompt: A vendor claims "96% accuracy" for a tool. What does that headline number, on its own, fail to tell you?

options.label: Nothing — a well-measured aggregate number is sufficient on its own
Whether the errors are evenly distributed or concentrated in a specific condition or subgroup that matters to your client
The name of the vendor's test set

questions.explanation: The same logic applies to a suspiciously uniform data field in this module — an aggregate number, or a uniform distribution, can hide exactly the specific problem you'd need to ask about directly to find.

questions.from: Two modules back — What These Systems Can Actually Do
questions.prompt: What is a language model actually doing when it produces an answer?

options.label: Reading the input and verifying its conclusion against what it knows to be true
Predicting the statistically likely next text given the input and its training patterns — which can be right without ever having been verified
Looking up the answer in a database of stored, confirmed facts

questions.explanation: A model trained on Solstice's contaminated "routine" default would predict fluently and confidently — with nothing in its output signaling that the pattern it learned was a form default, not a clinical judgment.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The failure mode nobody put in the proposal
description: A risk section isn't a legal formality bolted onto a proposal — it's a discipline of naming plausible, specific failure modes before they happen, while the client can still decide whether to accept them.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a foreseeable, specific failure mode that a generic risk disclaimer would not have surfaced
Distinguish a real risk-naming discipline from a boilerplate disclaimer

contentSections.title: Naming the Risk Before You Commit

contentSections.body: A post-mortem, six months after a loan-modification triage tool went live at Anchorline Credit Union: the system began approving hardship modifications for a loan type — adjustable-rate second mortgages — that the underlying policy explicitly excluded from automated approval, because the exclusion lived in a separate compliance document the model was never actually shown. Nobody had done anything reckless. The proposal that scoped this project had a risk section. It listed "model accuracy may vary" and "data privacy must be maintained" — both true, both generic, and neither one would have prompted anyone to ask the one question that would have caught this: does the model's training data actually reflect every policy exclusion, or only the ones written into the main underwriting guide?

A risk section that lists generic categories — accuracy, privacy, bias — isn't doing the job this module is about. The actual discipline is naming plausible, specific failure modes for this particular process, this particular client, before the engagement starts: what could actually go wrong here, given exactly what this automation touches and exactly what data and policy it's built from?

This is achievable, not a matter of predicting the unpredictable. Anchorline's specific failure — an exclusion living in a document the model never saw — was foreseeable the moment someone asked "where does every policy rule this system needs to honor actually live, and did all of it make it into what the model was built from?" That's a question a careful risk-naming pass would surface before the engagement, not a question that could only be answered in hindsight after the failure happened.

contentSections.scenario: Anchorline's original proposal's risk section, in full: "As with any AI system, model accuracy may vary over time, and data privacy must be maintained throughout the engagement in accordance with applicable regulations."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this risk section, beyond simply being short?

options.label: It states true things about AI projects in general, but names no failure mode specific to this process, this client, or this data — so it wouldn't have prompted anyone to ask the one question that would have caught the actual failure
It's too technical for a non-technical client to understand
It should have been a numbered list instead of a paragraph

feedback.generic-not-specific: Right. Both sentences are true and would appear, nearly word for word, in almost any AI project's risk section regardless of what the project actually does — which is exactly the problem. A risk section that would read the same for a chatbot, a fraud detector, and a loan-modification tool hasn't actually engaged with what could go wrong in this specific one, and it gives the client nothing to actually evaluate or ask a follow-up question about.
feedback.too-technical: The opposite is closer to true — the section is written in plain, accessible language. Accessibility isn't the problem; specificity is.
feedback.wrong-format: Formatting isn't the substantive issue here. A numbered list of the same two generic sentences would have the identical flaw.

contentSections.mechanism: A risk section does real work only when it names a plausible, specific failure mode tied to the actual process, data, and policy being automated — something a client could read and either recognize as a real concern or push back on with a specific fact you didn't have. Generic disclaimers about accuracy and privacy are true of nearly every AI project and specific to none of them, which means they can't do the one job a risk section actually has: making a foreseeable failure visible while there's still time to prevent it.

contentSections.scenario: You're reviewing draft risk sections for five different automation proposals, deciding which actually name a specific, foreseeable failure mode versus which are generic disclaimers dressed up as risk analysis.
contentSections.question: Select every risk-section entry that names a genuinely specific, foreseeable failure mode.

items.label: "The model was trained on the main underwriting guide but not the separate compliance addendum listing loan-type exclusions — if any exclusion isn't reflected in training data, the model may approve a case policy prohibits"

"At the proposed confidence threshold, roughly 1 in 20 auto-approved claims in our test sample would have been flagged for review by a human adjuster — that rate should be weighed against the cost of a wrongly approved claim at this dollar range"

"This pipeline depends on the vendor's API remaining available; based on their published uptime history, expect roughly N hours of unplanned downtime per quarter, during which the manual fallback process needs to be ready"
"Model accuracy may vary over time"
"Data privacy must be maintained in accordance with applicable regulations"
"AI systems can sometimes exhibit bias"

explanation.specific-exclusion: Applicable. This names the exact mechanism of a plausible failure — a specific document that might not be reflected in training data — giving the client something concrete to check or ask about before signing.
explanation.specific-volume: Applicable. This gives an actual number, tied to the actual proposed threshold and the actual dollar stakes, that the client can weigh — not a vague acknowledgment that errors are possible.
explanation.specific-dependency: Applicable. This names a specific, checkable dependency (vendor uptime) and its real consequence (needing the manual fallback ready), rather than a general statement that "technology can fail."
explanation.generic-accuracy: Not applicable. True of nearly every AI project, tells the client nothing to check or prepare for, and would read identically regardless of what this specific system does.
explanation.generic-privacy: Not applicable, for the same reason — this is a category label, not a named failure mode with a mechanism the client could evaluate.
explanation.generic-bias: Not applicable. "Can sometimes exhibit bias" names no specific mechanism, no specific population at risk, and no specific consequence — it's true and useless in the same way as the other two generic entries.

contentSections.synthesis: The three genuine entries all share a shape: a specific mechanism (an untrained exclusion, a known error rate, a vendor dependency), tied to this project specifically, with something the client can actually do about it (check the document, weigh the rate against the stakes, prepare the fallback). The three generic entries are true of nearly any AI project and give the client nothing to act on — which is the tell that a risk section is decorative rather than doing real work.

contentSections.body: A risk section does real work only when it names a specific, plausible failure mode tied to this process, this data, and this client — something the client could recognize, question, or prepare for. Generic disclaimers about accuracy, privacy and bias are true of almost every AI project and specific to none of them, which is exactly why they don't catch the failure that actually happens.

title: Silent failure versus loud failure, and which is worse
description: Two designs can have the same average error rate and need completely different mitigation in a proposal, because one fails in a way everyone notices immediately and the other fails in a way that looks exactly like success.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a design that fails loudly from one that fails silently, at the level of the proposal's risk section, not just the runtime code
Recommend proportionate mitigation for each failure type rather than uniform mitigation regardless of failure shape

contentSections.title: Two designs, same error rate, different risk

contentSections.body: Two competing designs for Anchorline's loan-modification triage reach the same measured error rate in testing — roughly 3%. Design A: when the model's confidence is below a threshold, it throws a visible flag and routes the case to a queue nobody can miss, with the case marked "needs manual review" in bold on every dashboard that touches it. Design B: the model always returns a decision with no confidence signal exposed downstream at all — a wrong decision looks, to every system and person that sees it afterward, identical to a right one. Both designs are 3% wrong. They are not equally risky, and a risk section that doesn't distinguish them hasn't actually done its job.

This is the proposal-level version of a distinction this track has made about individual AI outputs, applied now to entire system designs: a design that fails loudly announces its own errors somewhere a person or process will see them, bounding how long a wrong decision goes uncaught. A design that fails silently produces a wrong decision that looks, structurally, identical to a right one — nothing downstream signals anything went wrong, so the error persists until something entirely unrelated (a customer complaint, an audit, a lawsuit) surfaces it, potentially much later and at much larger scale.

The risk-section consequence: loud failure needs mitigation aimed at making sure the visible flag actually gets acted on (which connects back to the meaningful-review design from earlier in this track) — the failure announces itself, the job is making sure someone's listening. Silent failure needs a fundamentally different kind of mitigation: building in a detection mechanism where none exists naturally, because nothing about the design itself will ever surface the problem on its own.

contentSections.scenario: Three more design choices for Anchorline's system: (1) the model logs its confidence score internally, but no dashboard, alert, or downstream process ever reads that log; (2) the model refuses to produce a decision at all when confidence is very low, returning an explicit "unable to determine" status the case-management system is built to catch and route to a person; (3) the model always returns a specific modification amount, with no way for downstream systems to distinguish a high-confidence recommendation from a low-confidence guess.
contentSections.question: Which of these three is closest to design A (loud failure) from the hook — genuinely announcing uncertain cases somewhere they'll be caught?

options.label: Option 2 — the explicit "unable to determine" status the case-management system is built to catch
Option 1 — logging a confidence score internally
Option 3 — always returning a specific amount with no confidence signal

feedback.option2: Right. An explicit "unable to determine" status that a downstream system is specifically built to catch and route is exactly what loud failure means — the uncertainty produces a visible, actionable signal, not just a data point sitting somewhere unread.
feedback.option1: This looks like it should count, but it doesn't function as loud failure — a confidence score that nothing downstream ever reads behaves, in practice, identically to no confidence score existing at all. The information technically exists; it never reaches anyone who could act on it.
feedback.option3: This is the clearest silent-failure case of the three — with no way to distinguish a confident recommendation from a low-confidence guess, a wrong amount looks exactly like a right one to every system and person downstream.

contentSections.concept: Loud failure isn't defined by whether uncertainty information exists somewhere in the system — it's defined by whether that information reaches a person or process positioned to act on it before the decision takes effect. A logged-but-unread confidence score and a design with no confidence score at all fail in the same practical way, even though only one of them looks, on a system diagram, like it's tracking uncertainty.

contentSections.body: A proposal's risk section shouldn't recommend the same mitigation regardless of which failure shape a step has. For a loud-failure design, the mitigation is largely about the human process on the receiving end — is the flag actually monitored, does someone own responding to it, does the workload allow real attention (the same territory as this track's earlier work on meaningful review). For a silent-failure design, the mitigation has to be built into the system itself, because there's no natural point where a person would otherwise notice: a sampling audit that specifically checks outcomes against ground truth, a secondary model or rule that cross-checks a subset of decisions, or redesigning the step to surface a confidence signal in the first place, converting a silent-failure design into a loud-failure one before it ever ships.

Two designs with the same average error rate can carry very different risk depending on whether a wrong decision announces itself or looks identical to a right one. A risk section should name which shape a step has and recommend the mitigation that shape actually needs — a monitored human queue for loud failure, a built-in audit mechanism for silent failure — not a single generic mitigation applied uniformly regardless of how the failure would actually show up.

title: Regulated processes and the questions to ask first
description: Before scoping any automation in a regulated domain, a short set of first questions — which regulator, what obligations, what's already been reviewed, what audit trail is required — has to be asked and answered, because the answers change what's even possible to propose.

learningObjectives.text: Ask the first-order questions needed to scope an automation in a regulated process, before any design work begins
Recognize when a regulatory constraint changes what's possible to propose, not just what mitigation to add afterward

contentSections.title: The questions that come before scoping

contentSections.body: Anchorline's loan-modification process is subject to fair lending regulation, and the consultant scoping this engagement asks a set of questions before writing a single line of the proposal — not after the design is done, when reworking it would be far more expensive. Which regulator has jurisdiction here, and has Anchorline's compliance team already reviewed automated decisioning in this specific process, or would this be a first? What obligations does that regulator impose specifically on automated or algorithmic decisions, as opposed to general lending obligations that predate any automation question? What audit trail would that regulator expect to see if this decision were ever challenged? Getting these answers before scoping isn't due diligence theater — the answers change what's actually possible to propose, not just what disclaimer to add to an otherwise-unchanged plan.

A short, real checklist of first questions for any regulated process, asked before scoping begins: **Which regulator has jurisdiction, and has this client's compliance function already reviewed automated decisioning here, or is this the first time?** A client with existing internal review infrastructure for this kind of decision is a very different engagement than one for whom this would be the first automated decision in a regulated area. **What obligations apply specifically to automated or algorithmic decisions**, which are often stricter or different in kind from the general regulatory obligations that applied before any automation was proposed — adverse-action notice requirements, explainability requirements, fair-treatment testing obligations that a purely human process may have satisfied differently. **What audit trail would the regulator expect**, because a system that can't produce one may be unusable in this process regardless of how accurate it is — this connects directly to the debuggability criterion from earlier in this track, now framed as a hard external requirement rather than an internal preference. **Has legal or compliance signed off on automating this specific decision at all**, independent of any specific design — sometimes the honest first answer is that the client's own compliance function hasn't yet decided whether automation is permissible here, which is a fact that belongs in the engagement's very first conversation, not discovered in week six.

contentSections.scenario: You're scoping the Anchorline engagement and deciding what to ask before any design work begins.
contentSections.question: Select every question that belongs in this first-questions checklist, before scoping begins.

items.label: Which regulator has jurisdiction over this specific process, and has automated decisioning in it been reviewed before?
What obligations apply specifically to automated decisions here, as distinct from the general obligations that predate any automation question?
What audit trail would the regulator expect to see if a specific decision were challenged?
What programming language or cloud provider the client's engineering team prefers
How quickly the client would like the project delivered
How many people are on the client's engineering team

explanation.regulator-jurisdiction: Applicable. Whether this would be the client's first automated decision in a regulated area versus an area with existing review infrastructure changes the entire shape of what's achievable and how long it should realistically take.
explanation.automated-specific-obligations: Applicable. Regulatory obligations specific to automated decisions — like adverse-action notice or explainability requirements — can be materially different from what a human-run version of the same process was subject to, and missing this distinction is exactly how Anchorline's original engagement missed a real exclusion.
explanation.audit-trail-expectation: Applicable. If the regulator would expect a specific kind of audit trail and the proposed design can't produce it, that's a design-changing fact, not a footnote to add later — this needs answering before scoping locks in an approach that can't satisfy it.
explanation.preferred-tech-stack: Not applicable to this specific checklist — a real project consideration, but it doesn't touch what's regulatorily possible or required, which is what this checklist is specifically about.
explanation.project-timeline-preference: Not applicable here. Timeline preference is a real scoping input for other purposes, but it doesn't change what's legally required or permissible in a regulated process.
explanation.team-size: Not applicable. Client team size is relevant to staffing and handover planning elsewhere in an engagement, not to the regulatory first-questions this lesson is about.

contentSections.synthesis: The three questions that belong here all determine what's actually possible or required before any design work is worth doing — jurisdiction and prior review history, obligations specific to automation, and audit-trail expectations. The three that don't are real project-planning inputs, just not ones that change what a regulated process legally permits or requires, which is the specific gap this lesson is about closing before scoping rather than after.

contentSections.body: In a regulated process, the first questions — which regulator, what obligations apply specifically to automated decisions, what audit trail would be expected, has compliance already signed off — have to be asked before scoping, not folded into the risk section afterward, because the answers can change what's possible to propose at all, not just what disclaimer to add to an unchanged plan.

title: Writing risk into a proposal without losing the work
description: Naming a real risk honestly can read as a warning label that talks a client out of hiring you — the fix isn't softening the risk, it's pairing every named risk with a specific, credible mitigation that shows you've already thought about it.

learningObjectives.text: Write a risk-and-mitigation pairing that names a real risk honestly without reading as a reason not to proceed
Distinguish softening a risk from pairing it with a credible mitigation

contentSections.title: Honest risk, not a warning label

contentSections.body: A consultant drafts the risk section for Anchorline's rebuilt modification-triage proposal and gets nervous about one line: "If the model's training data doesn't fully reflect every policy exclusion, the system could approve a modification that violates policy." Read alone, that sentence sounds like a reason not to do the project at all — which is the opposite of what a good risk section should produce, since the whole discipline exists to make the engagement safer to proceed with, not scarier. The instinct to soften it ("the model is highly accurate and rarely makes mistakes") would defeat the entire purpose of this module. The actual fix isn't softening the risk — it's finishing the sentence with what specifically gets done about it.

The reframe that resolves this tension: a risk named without a mitigation reads as a warning label, because it implies the risk is simply being disclosed and left for the client to worry about. A risk paired with a specific, credible mitigation reads as evidence you've already thought carefully about the failure mode — which is a reason to hire you, not a reason not to.

The pairing needs both halves to actually be true. The risk has to be the real, specific one (not softened into vagueness), and the mitigation has to be a concrete, checkable action — not a reassurance. "The model could approve a policy-violating modification if an exclusion isn't reflected in training data" paired with "mitigation: every policy document, including compliance addenda, will be explicitly cross-referenced against training data coverage in stage 2, with any gap surfaced before the model is trained, not discovered after" does the actual job: it names the real risk, and it gives the client something specific to verify was done, rather than a promise to trust.

contentSections.code: A junior consultant's draft risk-and-mitigation pairing: "Risk: the model may occasionally produce an incorrect recommendation. Mitigation: we use industry-leading AI technology and follow best practices to minimize this risk."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this pairing?

options.label: Both halves are vague — the risk names no specific mechanism (which recommendation, in what situation), and the mitigation names no specific, checkable action, just reassuring language about quality
The risk is stated too alarmingly and should be softened further
The mitigation should come before the risk in the sentence

feedback.both-vague: Right. "May occasionally produce an incorrect recommendation" could describe literally any AI system doing any task — it names no mechanism specific to this engagement. "Industry-leading technology and best practices" is even worse: it's a reassurance with no checkable content at all, nothing the client could verify was actually done. A real pairing needs a specific risk mechanism and a specific, checkable mitigating action.
feedback.risk-too-scary: This has it backwards — the risk as written isn't specific enough to be scary or reassuring either way, because it doesn't name anything concrete. The problem is vagueness, not tone.
feedback.wrong-order: Ordering isn't the substantive issue — the same two vague sentences in either order would have identical problems.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A risk-and-mitigation pairing fails when either half could be copy-pasted into any other AI project's proposal unchanged. The fix for this pairing specifically: name the actual mechanism ("the model may misjudge modification requests involving loan types that are underrepresented in the training data") and a specific, checkable mitigation ("we will report per-loan-type accuracy from the validation set before go-live, and any loan type below the agreed threshold routes to mandatory human review") — something concrete enough that the client could actually check whether it happened.

contentSections.body: A named risk without a specific mitigation reads as a warning label. A named risk paired with a specific, checkable mitigation reads as evidence you've already thought about the failure — which is a reason to hire you, not a reason to walk away. The fix for a risk section that feels scary is never softening the risk; it's finishing the sentence with what specifically gets done about it.

title: Walking away, and how to do it professionally
description: Sometimes the honest risk-and-mitigation conversation ends with the client wanting to proceed without the mitigation — and the professional response is declining clearly, specifically, and in a way that leaves the relationship intact for work that doesn't have this problem.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a client's response to a named risk crosses from acceptable risk tolerance into a request you shouldn't do the work under
Decline an engagement specifically and professionally, preserving the relationship for other work

contentSections.title: "We hear the risk. Ship it anyway."

contentSections.body: Anchorline's project sponsor reads the risk section — the exclusion-coverage risk, the specific mitigation plan to cross-reference every policy document before training — and pushes back, not on the risk itself, but on the mitigation's timeline: "Cross-referencing every compliance addendum will add three weeks. Can we just ship with the main underwriting guide and add the addenda in a later phase?" This is a genuinely hard moment, because the request sounds reasonable on its face — phased delivery is normal — and it is also, specifically, a request to skip the exact mitigation that exists because of the exact failure mode this engagement's whole risk section was built to prevent.

The line between an acceptable risk tolerance and a request you shouldn't do the work under isn't about how the client phrases it — reasonable-sounding language ("just a later phase," "a small pilot first," "we'll monitor closely") can wrap a request that's functionally identical to removing the named mitigation for the named risk. The actual test: if the specific failure mode you named happens, will it happen inside this reduced scope, and does the client understand that it's the same risk, not a smaller version of it?

When the answer is yes — this is the same risk, not a reduced one, and the client wants to proceed without the mitigation anyway — declining is the professional, not the dramatic, response. Doing it well means being specific about what's being declined and why (not vague discomfort), naming exactly what would need to change for you to proceed, and doing it in a way that leaves the relationship intact for other work: the client isn't being told they're wrong to run their business this way, they're being told this specific piece of work, under these specific conditions, isn't something you can deliver responsibly — which is different, and can be said without either party losing face.

contentSections.title: Anchorline wants to skip the compliance-addenda cross-reference
contentSections.opening: The sponsor's request: ship using only the main underwriting guide, add the compliance addenda (including the adjustable-rate second-mortgage exclusion) in "phase 2," three weeks later.

reply.situation: You need to respond to the sponsor before the next planning call.
reply.question: What's the right first move?

choices.label: Agree, since phased delivery is a normal and reasonable request
choices.consequence: This treats the request as a scope-sequencing question, when it's actually a request to ship without the specific mitigation the risk section named for the specific failure mode already identified — the phase-2 framing doesn't change that the excluded loan type is live and unprotected for the full three weeks.

choices.label: Refuse without explanation, citing "policy"
choices.consequence: This is honest in outcome but gives the sponsor no way to understand what's actually being protected against, or what would change the answer — it reads as inflexibility rather than a reasoned professional judgment, and risks the relationship for no added benefit over a clear explanation.

choices.label: Point out specifically that this isn't a smaller version of the risk — the adjustable-rate second-mortgage exclusion is exactly the failure mode already named, and ask what alternative would actually address the timeline pressure without removing that specific protection
choices.consequence: You've named precisely what's being traded away, in the client's own terms, and opened a real conversation about alternatives instead of a binary yes or no.

alternatives.situation: The sponsor, once it's named specifically, says: "We didn't realize that exclusion was specifically what was at stake — we thought this was general caution. What are our actual options?"
alternatives.question: What do you propose?

choices.label: Propose narrowing phase 1's scope to exclude adjustable-rate second mortgages from automated decisioning entirely — those cases route to a human, everything else launches on schedule, and the addenda cross-reference for the narrower remaining risk happens in the original timeline
choices.consequence: This gives the sponsor most of the original timeline while removing the specific, named risk from what actually ships automated — the loan type most at risk simply isn't automated yet, rather than being automated without its exclusion being checked.

choices.label: Propose shipping on the original timeline, with a human spot-checking every adjustable-rate second-mortgage case manually until the addenda cross-reference finishes
choices.consequence: This also removes the actual risk — the loan type doesn't get an automated decision at all until it's protected, it gets a manual one, which was never the risky path in the first place.

shipped-risk.summary: A phased-delivery framing was accepted without recognizing it was functionally identical to removing the named mitigation — the excluded loan type is live and unprotected for the full three weeks, exactly the failure mode the original risk section existed to prevent.
shipped-risk.lesson: A request phrased as normal scope-sequencing can still be, functionally, a request to skip a specific named mitigation for a specific named risk — the test isn't how reasonable the phrasing sounds, it's whether the actual failure mode is still exposed in the reduced scope.

unexplained-refusal.summary: The risk itself doesn't ship, but the sponsor is left without a real explanation or a path forward, which damages the relationship more than a clear, specific answer would have and gives Anchorline no way to actually solve their timeline pressure.
unexplained-refusal.lesson: Declining professionally means being specific about what's being declined and why, and naming what would change the answer — not citing policy without explanation, which reads as inflexibility rather than professional judgment.

resolved.summary: The specific risk gets named in terms the sponsor actually understands, and a real alternative — narrowing scope or adding a manual check for exactly the exposed loan type — resolves the timeline pressure without shipping the named failure mode.
resolved.lesson: The professional response to a client wanting to skip a named mitigation isn't a binary yes or a flat no — it's naming precisely what's being traded away in terms they'll recognize, and proposing a real alternative that removes the actual risk rather than just its label.

contentSections.body: When a client wants to proceed without a named mitigation, the test isn't how reasonable their phrasing sounds — it's whether the actual failure mode is still exposed under what they're proposing. Naming that specifically, in the client's own terms, and proposing a real alternative is what makes declining (or renegotiating) professional rather than dramatic — and it's what keeps the relationship intact for work that doesn't have this problem.

Distinguish a real risk section from a generic disclaimer or an unactionable warning label

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Produce a Risk Register for a Proposed Automation
description: Take a real or realistic proposed automation and produce a risk register — specific failure modes, likelihood, impact, an owner, and a concrete mitigation per row — the kind a client could actually read and act on.

learningObjectives.text: Produce a risk register with specific, mechanism-level failure modes rather than generic categories
Pair every named risk with likelihood, impact, an owner, and a checkable mitigation

contentSections.body: Pick one real or realistically-detailed proposed automation you can reason about honestly — from your own work, a client's, or one you can research concretely enough. Produce the risk register for it: not generic categories, but specific, plausible failure modes tied to this process and this data, each with a likelihood, an impact, a named owner, and a mitigation specific enough that someone could check whether it actually happened.

contentSections.title: Your risk register
contentSections.brief: Choose one real proposed automation. Identify its genuinely plausible, specific failure modes — not generic AI-project disclaimers — and produce a full risk register a client could read before signing and actually act on.
contentSections.deliverable: A risk register: for each identified risk, a specific failure mode (mechanism, not category), likelihood, impact, an owner, and a concrete, checkable mitigation.

stages.title: Identify specific, plausible failure modes
stages.instructions: For your chosen automation, name 4-6 specific, plausible ways it could fail — tied to its actual data, process, and mechanism, the way Anchorline's untrained-exclusion risk was specific rather than a generic accuracy disclaimer. Reject any entry that would read the same for a different project.
stages.checkpoint: You have 4-6 failure modes, each naming a specific mechanism rather than a general category like "accuracy" or "bias."

stages.title: Classify failure shape and regulatory exposure
stages.instructions: For each risk, note whether it would fail loudly (self-announcing) or silently (indistinguishable from success without deliberate checking), and whether it touches a regulated process requiring specific first-questions answered.
stages.checkpoint: Every risk has a failure-shape classification, and any regulated-process risk notes what regulatory question it connects to.

stages.title: Assign likelihood, impact, owner and mitigation
stages.instructions: For each risk, estimate likelihood and impact (even roughly — high/medium/low with a one-sentence reason is fine), name a specific accountable owner, and write a mitigation specific and checkable enough that someone could verify it was actually done — not a reassurance.
stages.checkpoint: Every row has likelihood, impact, an owner, and a mitigation a reader could check off as done or not done.

stages.title: Self-check against the rubric
stages.instructions: Read back through the full register. For each row, ask: would this read identically if pasted into a different project's proposal? If yes, it isn't specific enough yet — revise it.
stages.checkpoint: No row in the register would be equally at home, unchanged, in an unrelated project's risk register.

rubric.criterion: Every risk names a specific mechanism, not a generic category
rubric.meets: The risk would not read identically if pasted into a different project's risk register.

rubric.criterion: Failure shape (loud vs. silent) is classified for each risk
rubric.meets: Each row states whether the failure would self-announce or require deliberate detection, with a one-sentence reason.

rubric.criterion: Regulatory exposure is noted where relevant
rubric.meets: Any risk touching a regulated process names the specific obligation or question it connects to.

rubric.criterion: Every risk has likelihood, impact, and a named owner
rubric.meets: All three fields are filled with real, specific content, not placeholders.

rubric.criterion: Every mitigation is concrete and checkable
rubric.meets: A reader could verify whether the mitigation was actually done, not just whether it was promised.

rubric.criterion: The register reads as evidence of careful thought, not a warning label
rubric.meets: Every risk is paired with its mitigation on the same row, per this module's risk-and-mitigation pairing principle.

contentSections.body: A risk register that lists generic categories with no specific mechanism, no failure-shape classification, and no checkable mitigation isn't a risk register — it's a disclaimer with a table around it. The version that actually protects a client, and actually helps you win the work, names the real, specific thing that could go wrong and exactly what's being done about it.

Whether the client is a long-standing relationship or a new one

questions.explanation: Anchorline's "phase 2" framing sounded like normal scope-sequencing but left the exact named failure mode — the untested exclusion — live and unprotected; the test is the actual exposure, not the phrasing.

questions.from: Previous module — The Data You Actually Have
questions.prompt: A field looks clean and consistent — the same distribution across every user and time period. Why might this be a warning sign rather than reassurance?

options.label: It isn't a warning sign — consistency is always good
Real, independent human judgments should show some natural variation — a rate that's identical everywhere is more consistent with a shared structural artifact than genuine judgment
It suggests the sample size is too small

questions.explanation: This is the same instinct this module's risk-naming work draws on — a suspiciously reassuring signal deserves the same scrutiny as a suspiciously alarming one.

questions.from: Previous module — The Data You Actually Have
questions.prompt: Before sending personal data to a third-party AI vendor, what's the first thing that needs checking?

options.label: Whether the vendor's product is technically accurate
Whether a data processing agreement is in place and what the vendor's actual data-use terms are, not their marketing claims
How much the vendor charges per API call

questions.explanation: This is exactly the kind of specific, checkable finding this module's risk register asks for, rather than a general reassurance about the vendor.

questions.from: Two modules back — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: What does a named accountable role actually need in order to provide real accountability, not just exist on an org chart?

options.label: A clear job title
Visibility into the specific disputed case, plus real authority to correct the decision
A fast response time to complaints

questions.explanation: This is the same standard a risk register's "owner" column has to meet — a named owner with no real visibility or authority is decorative, in a risk register just as much as in a review process.

questions.from: Two modules back — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: What actually determines whether a decision belongs in the class that needs a named human owner, regardless of average accuracy?

options.label: Whether the step runs at high volume
Whether a wrong decision changes what a specific person is owed, what care they receive, or what their record says, in a way that's hard to reverse
Whether the step is central to the company's revenue

questions.explanation: Anchorline's modification decisions sit squarely in this class, which is exactly why the risk register in this module's lab needs specific owners and mitigations, not generic ones.

questions.from: Three modules back — Rules, AI, or a Person
questions.prompt: Once accuracy is roughly comparable across mechanisms, what actually decides which one to use?

options.label: Whichever mechanism is the newest technology
Cost at real volume, latency requirements, and whether a specific decision needs to be explainable later
Whichever vendor has the best reputation

questions.explanation: Debuggability specifically reappears in this module as the regulatory audit-trail requirement — the same criterion, now framed as an external obligation rather than an internal preference.
